#4664. China’s super-secret space plane visible in clearest photo yet

Published Oct 27, 2026 2:51 PM EDT

The Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) has released the public’s best look yet at Shenlong, China’s ultra-secret space plane. Details remain scarce on the experimental reusable vehicle, but the unclassified photo offers an unprecedented glimpse of the craft from below, as well as clear views of its unique, rear-facing solar panel arrays.

The photo was taken in 2024 by the geospace intelligence company Maxar Technologies, and is wedged inside the DIA’s latest edition of its Challenges to Security in Space report. The 130-page threat assessment examines the biggest space-based issues currently facing the U.S. and its allies. Although the ever-growing cloud of orbital debris and junk above everyone’s heads remains an international problem, the report also focuses on the near- and long-term aims of countries like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.

Located on page 53 of the report, the photo’s caption simply describes it as an unnamed Chinese “spaceplane,” but it is almost certainly China’s second reusable orbital vehicle, Shenlong. Very little is known about the project even nearly 20 years after China officially revealed its existence. A Shenlong prototype launched on an initial two-day orbital mission in 2020, followed by a 276-day mission in 2022. Maxar’s 2024 photo coincides with the country’s third known, 268-day orbital test of Shenlong that launched in December 2023. According to the DIA, Shenlong “released and interacted with an object,” but good luck learning much else about it.

The mysterious space plane is reportedly engaged in a fourth excursion after launching from China’s Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on February 7, 2026. This places it alongside X-37B, the U.S. Space Force’s own secretive robot plane. Designed by Boeing, the reusable vehicle has spent 431 days and counting in low Earth orbit on its eighth classified mission. There is also a bit more available information on the solar-powered spaceplane. The vertical takeoff, horizontal-landing spaceplane measures over 29 feet long, features a nearly 15-foot-long wingspan, and reaches an orbital speed of 17,426 mph. Its full capabilities are unsurprisingly highly classified, although the U.S. Space Force did reveal its eighth mission includes testing cutting-edge laser communications technology as well as quantum measurement instruments.

#4663. BYD now has 1.02 million workers, more than Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla combined

BYD now has more than 1.02 million employees, according to chairman Wang Chuanfu. That’s more people than Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla employ combined.

And it’s a big jump from the start of the year. BYD reported about 869,600 employees at the end of 2025, which means the Chinese automaker has added roughly 150,000 people in 10 months while its vehicle sales are down.

Roughly 960,000 of BYD’s people work in China and about 60,000 work abroad. Up to 120,000 of them are R&D engineers, according to Wang, who shared the figures on stage Wednesday at the China Society of Automotive Engineers’ (CSAE) 33rd annual conference. Their work covers battery cells, motors, electronic controls, and semiconductors.

Wang credits vertical integration for that scale. In his telling, keeping batteries, chips, and motors in-house is what took BYD from a battery maker founded in 1994 to the world’s top-selling new energy vehicle brand several years running. He called the company’s rise a microcosm of China’s auto industry going from follower to leader.

BYD’s workforce has been all over the place in the last few years.

The company had about 570,100 employees at the end of 2022 and 703,500 at the end of 2023. Then it went on a hiring spree. We reported in September 2024 that BYD had passed 900,000 employees and claimed the largest R&D workforce of any automaker, with over 110,000 engineers. It ended 2024 with 968,900 people.

Then came the first big cut. BYD’s 2025 annual report showed roughly 869,600 employees at year-end, a drop of about 99,000, mostly in frontline production jobs.

Now it’s back over a million. Data compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence put BYD at 911,900 employees at the end of June, so the company added more than 100,000 people in about four months.

The gap with legacy automakers is massive. Volkswagen Group, which counts its Chinese joint ventures, reported 662,942 employees at the end of 2025. Toyota had 390,927 as of March 31, 2026, and Stellantis had 258,668 at the end of last year.

In the US, Ford ended 2025 with 169,000 employees and GM with 156,000. Tesla reported a worldwide headcount of 134,785 in its latest 10-K.

Add up Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla and you get about 851,000 people. BYD has roughly 170,000 more than that.

But headcount isn’t output. If you divide 2025 global vehicle sales by year-end workforce, BYD comes out far behind:

BYD sold about 4.6 million vehicles last year with 869,600 employees, or 5.3 vehicles per worker. Tesla delivered 1,636,129 vehicles with 134,785 people, about 12 per worker, and Volkswagen Group was at about 13.5. Toyota, with 11.3 million group sales including Daihatsu and Hino, got roughly 29 vehicles out of each employee.

There’s a catch, and it’s a big one. BYD’s headcount isn’t only a car company’s headcount. It includes BYD Electronic, its majority-owned contract manufacturer that assembles devices for other brands and reported 165,000 employees of its own at the end of 2025. It also covers BYD’s battery business, which supplies other automakers, plus its in-house chips, motors, energy storage, and rail transit operations.

In short, BYD’s vertical integration largely drives its high headcount.

BYD sold 3,131,576 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, down 3.9% year-over-year. September was its best month of the year at 463,561 units, but the company has been stuck in a brutal price war at home and is losing ground to rivals like Geely and Leapmotor. Its first-half revenue (344.8 billion yuan) and net profit (12.3 billion yuan) were both down year-over-year.

All of the growth is overseas. BYD’s international sales hit 1,342,960 units through September, up 92.7%, and they now make up about 43% of its total volume. That’s on top of BYD beating Tesla on pure EV deliveries again in Q2.

Yet only 60,000 of its 1.02 million workers are based outside China. That’s about 6%. So BYD is still building nearly everything at home and shipping it out, even as its factories in Thailand, Brazil, and Hungary come online.

The 1.02 million number makes for a great headline, but we wouldn’t read it as a sign of strength on its own.

BYD doesn't just make cars. It makes a lot of battery and other parts that go into other things such as other automaker's EVs.

It is automakers, auto supplier, battery makers, electronic contract manufacturer all merged into one.

Remember GM used to make refrigerators and satellites in addition to cars at one point.

BYD’s whole model is to make almost everything itself: cells, chips, motors, seats, and a lot more. That’s a big reason it can sell a Seagull for around $10,000 in China and still make money. But it’s a labor-heavy model, and it works because Chinese factory labor is relatively cheap and plentiful. Toyota gets more than five times as many cars out of each employee. Tesla gets more than twice as many.

The problem is that BYD’s growth is now outside China, and that’s where this model gets tested. Only 6% of its workforce is abroad, yet 43% of its sales are. Tariffs in Europe, Brazil, Mexico, and elsewhere are pushing BYD to build locally, but a factory in Hungary or Brazil won’t necessarily produce the same.

The number that should worry legacy automakers is the 120,000 engineers. That’s almost as many people as Tesla employs in total, all working on product.

#4662. A Meeting With Elizabeth Holmes

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Like many Americans, I recently watched You Can See Everything, the documentary that follows Elizabeth Holmes through the weeks before she reported to prison. I left the theater fascinated and bewildered. Throughout the movie, I kept asking the same question the filmmakers seem to be asking: Am I being deceived, or am I missing something because I don't know enough?

I have asked myself that question about Holmes before. In July 2013, I was the Deputy Commissioner for the New York City Health Department, where I oversaw the city's infectious disease programs and the public health laboratory. City Hall asked me to meet with a promising new lab-testing company; a few weeks later, I joined an hour-long video call with Holmes, her team, and our lab director.

I still have my notes. Holmes and her colleagues told us that their company, Theranos, had developed a more convenient way to test blood in small amounts that would cut testing costs by 30 percent.

A wide range of tests had been validatedFederal and New York State regulatory approvals were completeThey secured a Department of Defense contract. Testing was scheduled to launch at New York Walgreens pharmacies within months.

My colleague and I asked repeatedly about the underlying science and data. Every time, we got the same answer: they could not disclose business secrets, but everything worked and was approved. Rest assured.

When the call ended, my colleague and I were dumbfounded. Nothing we knew about collecting specimens, validating tests, or getting regulatory approval made their story plausible. And yet I doubted myself. Holmes spoke with such composure and certainty and had such powerful connections and investors that I kept wondering: Did she know something about science or lab regulations that I didn't?

We offered to evaluate the device in our lab before any wider use. Neither side ever followed up. When the Wall Street Journal published its first investigation into the company in October 2015, I called my colleague, and we both said the same thing: "We knew it!" Most of what she said in that meeting was not true.

After watching the movie, I kept thinking about that incident and how it raised a hard healthcare problem: knowing when to trust your own expertise and when to defer to someone else's.

We assume that people who sound certain know more than we do. This is particularly common when checking a person’s claims is difficult or costly. That describes the Theranos meeting almost exactly. We could not check her claims because she said her data was confidential, and she spoke with absolute certainty.

While the lack of data made me suspicious, I fell prey to something known as “the halo effect,” where people with credibility in one domain are often thought to be credible experts in other domains. Theranos had funders and board members who had extremely prestigious backgrounds in government and the military. Even though none of them had a background in laboratory medicine, I assumed they had done sufficient due diligence on the technology.

A big challenge in health: The body is so complex that none of us can be experts in everything. As a physician, if I order an MRI on a patient, I rely on the radiologist to interpret it correctly. When I order a blood test, I rely on laboratory technicians to use validated methods and equipment. I could not do my job if I had to personally verify that everyone knows what they are doing and is doing it correctly. The need to trust others is even greater for patients, because most of them will not be medical experts.

The problem, of course, is that humans are imperfect. Medical errors are, unfortunately, quite common. Someone did something wrong—errors of commission; someone forgot to do something—errors of omission. And, because medical knowledge is always growing, something correct 10 years ago may be incorrect now. I always encourage people to ask their healthcare providers questions and, with major health decisions, to seek second opinions.

How do you decide when and whom to trust? Here are a few questions you can ask whether you are a patient talking to a doctor or interpreting health claims online.

First, is this an area where you have real knowledge and experience? If so, give your own judgment more weight than you are inclined to, even when the person across from you is more confident than you are.

Second, does their authority come from the relevant field? A famous name, a large social media following, or impressive business credentials do not mean they understand how a vaccine works or what a blood test measures.

Third, is the other person offering evidence or only certainty? Consider asking, “What is the evidence that supports this approach? Is this what expert guidelines recommend?” Trustworthy experts can explain their reasoning or point you to high-quality studies or published guidelines to check their claims.

Fourth, has anyone independently checked? Has it been approved by the FDA or another government regulatory agency? Or do major professional organizations recommend it?

We need our health experts and institutions to see everything—the methods and the data—to make sure medications, vaccines, and other health interventions are safe and effective. But when someone asks for our trust and won’t back it up with data, we need to consider trusting our own judgment or asking for a second opinion.

#4661. Why are bogs so good at preserving dead bodies?

Published Oct 27, 2026 3:43 PM EDT

In August of 1984, commercial peat cutters working near Wilmslow, about a half-hour drive south of Manchester, England, discovered a dead body in the moss. The corpse was determined to be a 25-year-old man with a closely shorn beard and well-manicured nails. He had suffered two or three heavy blows to the head, and had sustained a cut throat and a fractured rib. But this wasn’t a fresh corpse: His body had been laying in that peat bog for nearly 2,000 years.

The “Lindow Man” is just one of at least 2,000 bog bodies recovered from Europe’s peatlands. They date from the Mesolithic period, which ended in Europe between 8,500 to 5,500 years ago, all the way up through World War II.

“Bog bodies” are essentially human corpses that peat bogs have naturally preserved and mummified. Quite often, their skin, hair, nails, and internal organs are remarkably intact for thousands of years. Their bones, however, are a whole other story.

To find out more about why bogs are so good at preserving bodies, Popular Science turned to author Anna North, a journalist whose fascination with peat bogs and preserved “bog bodies” inspired her national bestseller Bog Queen. This eco-historical mystery novel details what happens when a forensic anthropologist starts investigating a well-preserved Iron Age bog body, and required extensive research on North’s part. The author first got the idea for her book after coming across the Lindow Man at London’s British Museum, where he’s on permanent display.

“He doesn’t look great,” she says, “but he’s just so recognizably still a human.” The fact that North was sharing a room with this person who ate, drank, and walked the earth 2,000 years ago left an indelible mark on her. She wanted to learn more. “One of the first things I realized is that I didn’t have a good sense of what a peat bog would even look like.”

A bog or “peat bog” is an acidic, nutrient-poor wetland ecosystem. It’s made up of peat, which is ground that’s soft and spongy and consists of partially decayed plant material that builds up over hundreds or thousands of years.

“Peat is really any kind of organic matter that builds up faster than it decays,” says North. It can be grasses, reeds, roots, and shrubs. But peat mostly consists of Sphagnum moss, a large group of shaggy-looking, moisture-loving mosses.

“Sphagnum moss has the capacity to take in a lot of water and store it, so it becomes really spongy and waterlogged.” This creates an excellent environment for preservation, says North, “because there’s not much air.”

While bogs exist across the globe, you’ll find them mostly in cool, northern climates with lots of rain. For years, these mysterious landscapes have appeared as ominous settings in literature. They’re especially popular in Victorian detective fiction and gothic novels like Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s The Hounds of the Baskervilles and Daphne du Maurier’s Jamaica Inn. And for good reason. Their mist-shrouded surfaces (a result of the cool, damp air that sits above their spongy terrain), unstable footing, and stagnant waters make them natural backdrops for the unknown. Of course, there are also the bodies.

The preservation of bog bodies results from a highly-detailed balance of water source, chemistry, and vegetation.

Bogs get almost all of their water from rain and snow, which makes them low in minerals and nutrients. The water also doesn’t move thanks to the bog’s sponge-like moss.

Thick layers of decomposed organic material choke off the air supply to the decaying plant matter underneath. Without oxygen, the environment becomes highly acidic and aerobic bacteria and fungi are unable to thrive. This means they can’t break down that dead plant (and human) material the way they normally would.

Instead, the bog’s high acidity essentially “pickles” human corpses, many of which were left behind as part of a ritual sacrifice or the result of executions. The environment’s low pH (the result of its high acidity) acts like a pickle juice brine, stopping harmful bacteria from growing and preserving bodies almost like “living time capsules.” Sphagnum moss also releases a complex carbohydrate that binds to the proteins in human skin and tissue, called sphagnan. This carbohydrate turns the skin leathery and a dark-brown “tea” color while protecting it against decay. But while this unique environment slows a body’s decomposition, the bog’s intense acid leaches the calcium right out of human bones.

“If you look at X-rays of bog bodies, they’re not going to look like an X-ray of a living person,” says North. Mostly because the bones are softened, warped, or have dissolved completely.

Raised bogs, which are deep, dome-shaped peatlands that are both wetter and higher than their surrounding lands, are best at preserving bodies. That’s because they’re both highly acidic and entirely void of oxygen.

The shallower peat found in blanket bogs means that bodies decompose faster (though bog bodies are still found here). Fens, which are peat-accumulating wetlands that both  surface water and mineral-rich groundwater replenish, are less acidic. This means that a body’s soft-tissue will typically decay.

One way that forensic anthropologists can typically tell the difference between a recently decreased person and a bog body is through their teeth. While researching for her book, North discovered that people who lived and died before there was refined flour would have really different patterns of tooth decay than modern-day eaters.

Back then, she says, “They might actually grind wheat or corn with stone, and little bits of stone would end up in their flour. Those people would then chew on that stone and it would grind down their teeth.”

Cremation or casket? Here’s the most eco-friendly burial option.

What happens when you donate your body to science?

How human composting turns bodies into soil

Some people really are werewolves—at least, in their minds

What happens to your body when you die in space?

North also learned that identifying a bog body is a collaborative effort. A bioarchaeologist, who studies human biological remains at archaeological sites, might be brought in to determine the corpse’s age and sex, while a pathologist would examine the cause of death.

“It turns out that the same process that makes bogs really good at preserving a body also means that they’re storing this enormous amount of carbon,” says North.

Since there’s no oxygen to break down a bog’s organic plant matter, it just piles up layer by layer forming thick, carbon-rich peat. In fact, peatlands (including bogs) only cover roughly three-perfect of the planet’s land surface, though they store twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests combined. “They’re just a really powerful resource.”

Bogs are generally safe to walk across as well, despite their reputation for being “graveyards” of sorts. “There are cases of people appearing to have accidentally died on bogs,” says North. “Still, if you’re an average person visiting a bog today and you stay on the marked trail, I am not concerned for your safety.”

Forget about the 600+ hp hybrid-powered Polestar 1 supercoupe; the car that established Polestar as a standalone brand was the 2. As the brand pulls out of the US and shifts its focus to the rest of the world, it’s time to look back at the EV that helped define Polestar, along with a look around at some of the best EV deals of all time.

A number of European news sites (including Electrive and TV2 Broom) are reporting that the last new Polestar 2 has rolled off the company’s Luqiao assembly line, with more than 200,000 of the all-electric sedan/hatchbacks built in China since the electric sedan launched in 2020. And, while the company hasn’t confirmed that with any sort of official announcement, the news jives with the company’s previously announced plans to release an updated Polestar 2 in 2027, followed by an all-new Polestar 7 SUV that’s set to follow in early 2028.

With the brand set to pull out of the US after the Trump Administration’s Commerce Department declined to grant it authorization under the Connected Vehicle Rule earlier this year, it might at first seem like that US Polestar fans will miss out on that freshened 2, whatever shape it takes – but don’t lose hope, yet.

First shown in 2016, the original Volvo Concept 40.2 was supposed to be a new, entry-level sedan for the now Geely-owned Volvo, which was in the process of separating itself from Ford ownership and the Focus-based C30 coupe and S40/V50 sedan and wagons. And a fine entry-level Volvo it would have been, too, if Tesla’s share price hadn’t made it worth more than the next five most valuable car companies combined.

See, once Tesla (or, more to the point, $TSLA) did that, every carmaker in the world figured the stock market would bless them with billions, too, and started announcing plans to go all electric, right now. Volvo parent company Geely, however, decided they’d fast-track the process, taking the next two Volvo models in their pipeline (the C90 coupe version of the S90 sedan and the C40 sedan previewed by the Concept 40.2) and made them Polestars.

A SPAC merger later, and Polestar was spun off as not only its own brand, but its own, largely Chinese-owned company – which brings us to where we are now.

In the US the Polestar 3 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) SUV starts at something like $67,500 and offers a 111 kWh battery pack good for an EPA-rated range of up to 350 miles. The top-shelf Performance-spec Polestar 3, meanwhile, offers an all-wheel-drive dual-motor setup that Polestar rates at 380 kW (~517 hp) that will launch you across suburbia with a 0–60 mph time in the 4 second range, albeit with slightly less range than the base model … but that $67,500 price is really more of a suggestion these days.

Polestar is offering a $23,000 discount on the 3 and a $25,000, rebate, market adjustment or whatever on the 4. That means that you can get a brand new Polestar 3 or 4 with Chinese EV tech and more than a little bit of Volvo safety baked in for a dramatically reduced price. If you pick the right one at the right dealer, probably for less than $40,000.

One of the best looking cars from the last decade… the 2024+ RWD is such a great value…. I got one myself a year ago for $28k with 5k on the odometer.

As for the 2, I have a bit of a personal connection to that one. My son picked up a 19,000 mile 2024 Polestar 2 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) in Glacier for under $22K, which is an absolutely shocking price for a fast, capable sporty sedan hatchback that isn’t just a worthy successor to the S40 it was meant to replace, but a solid foundation for an EV brand that got wrapped up in politics.

#4659. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4658. Unknown bald eagle spotted on Shadow’s nest

Published Oct 27, 2026 4:18 PM EDT

The bald eagle nest in Big Bear Valley has welcomed a new visitor. On Tuesday, cameras spotted an unknown adult spending time in the nest once shared by Jackie and Shadow.

The new eagle was first seen last week, but returned on Tuesday for about 30 minutes to fiddle with a few sticks and pose in front of the nest cam operated by Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV). A sub-adult eagle has also been spotted on FOBBV’s cameras in recent weeks. Shadow has not been seen by the cameras since October 23. Kaydee, a young adult bald eagle who has been seen arranging sticks and singing with Shadow in the past few months, was last seen on October 21.

It’s not unusual for bald eagles to spend less time in their nests in the fall. Fans often refer to this time as “bald eagle vacation,” where the birds will spend time exploring other parts of the area and sleeping in trees with more cover. Mating season for the Big Bear Valley bald eagles typically starts in December. It’s not yet known if Shadow will return to his nest or mate with a new partner following the death of Jackie on August 10.

Jackie and Shadow were not the original inhabitants of the nest seen on the FOBBV cams. Jackie’s parents, Lucy and Ricky, built the nest during the 2012-2013 nesting season. Shortly after the 2011-2012 nesting season, when Jackie was born and eventually fledged, Lucy and Ricky’s old nest blew away in a strong storm.

The old nest sat at the top of a dead tree. The new nest occupied a nearby, stronger tree about 50 feet away from where Jackie was raised. Lucy and Ricky abandoned the nest in the 2015-2016 season, opting instead to build a new nest nearby. At the beginning of the 2016-2017 nesting season, Lucy and Ricky disappeared from the area. It’s unknown where they went or what happened to them. But that same season, a juvenile female began hanging out at their old pad. Experts later guessed this was Jackie. She used this nest, first with original partner Mr. B and later with Shadow, until her death.

In summer 2026, Shadow continued to tend to the nest with the pair’s chicks, Sandy and Luna, until they fledged in mid-July. In the months that followed, he continued to visit the nest and eventually allowed Kaydee to also spend time there.

Stay tuned to the FOBBV cameras to see how this bald eagle story continues to unfold. Camera 1 (the main nest cam) is currently running its usual 24/7 streaming schedule, but Camera 2 (the wide angle) is currently being turned off at night to conserve energy.

#4657. Postpartum Prevention Plan: Time Outside, Exercise, Socialize

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Postpartum depression and anxiety are major issues that affect new caregivers. Many new parents focus on the birth plan to prepare for this major stage of life. But what I find in my work as a clinical psychologist is that new families really benefit from a postpartum plan as well. What are the needs, relationships, and activities that will help you maintain your well-being postpartum? Knowing these will promote your child’s well-being as well. I developed the following mnemonic to capture core helpful practices that are supported by research: Time Outside, Exercise, and Socialize. These three practices can provide a daily structure that maximizes joy during a time that is challenging but also fulfilling.

1. Time Outside: Follow the mantra often told to caregivers of newborns — leave the house every day. Time spent in nature has been associated with enhanced mood, emotional regulation, optimism, resilience, and child development (Hall et al., 2023). Research on mothers and nature has attested to the benefits of the outdoors on postnatal well-being and the relief it provides from indoor stressors (Hall et al., 2023). Getting out is key. Even if being in nature isn't possible, go out for coffee, lunch, or to a museum to provide novelty and stimulation that can vary your routine and perk up the day. Physicians have dispelled myths that you shouldn’t leave home with your newborn, as fresh air and a change of scenery are beneficial to both parent and child well-being (Davis, 2015).

2. Exercise: If you are able to, getting some kind of walk in every day with a newborn is not only good for you but also for your child. Strap them into a carrier of your choosing or affix a stroller with all the things you might need to leave the house for an hour. A meta-analysis reviewing a wide range of studies found that exercise alone (without the use of other interventions) is effective in reducing postpartum depression and anxiety (Deprato et al., 2025). A moderate reduction in the severity of symptoms was achieved through at least 80 minutes a week of rigorous exercise, which could include a brisk walk, swimming, cycling, and other activities.

3. Socialize: Invite a friend or family member for a visit or walk. Attend a local baby-friendly gathering that can take you and an infant out into the world, like a yoga, music, play, or story time group. Research suggests that social interaction is a powerful protective factor in preventing postpartum depression and anxiety (Feinberg et al., 2022). Another study found that social support is particularly important for women who are at risk of postpartum mental health problems, such as those with more than one child, pregnancy loss, negative body image, and a history of mental health problems.

It is important to note that all three of these components overlap — socializing, time outside, and exercise could all take place during a long walk with a friend. But if you are having trouble getting out with the baby, have others help you, if possible, so you don’t have to make this happen on your own. And if consistent practice of these activities doesn’t seem to help, reaching out to a medical and/or mental health professional is essential. Severe cases of postpartum depression and anxiety may be resistant to daily health behaviors, but professional treatment is still effective. More support is available at the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline (1-833-852-6262) and Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773).

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Davis, S. (2015). Can I take my newborn outside? https://www.webmd.com/parenting/baby/features/can-i-take-my-newborn-outside

Deprato, A., Ruchat, S. M., Ali, M. U., Cai, C., Forte, M., Gierc, M., Meyer, S., Sjwed, T. N., Shirazi, S., Matenchuk, B. A., Jones, P. A. T., Sivak, A., & Davenport, M. H. (2025). Impact of postpartum physical activity on maternal depression and anxiety: A systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 59(8), 550–561. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2024-108478

Feinberg, E., Declercq, E., Lee, A., & Belanoff, C. (2022). The relationship between social support and postnatal anxiety and depression: Results from the Listening to Mothers in California survey. Women's Health Issues, 32(3), 251–260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.whi.2022.01.005

Hall, K., Evans, J., Roberts, R., Brown, R., Barnes, C., & Turner, K. (2023). Mothers' accounts of the impact of being in nature on postnatal wellbeing: a focus group study. BMC Women's Health, 23(1), 32. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12905-023-02165-x

#4656. New Trek e-bike is first to get Bosch’s new motor with a major power upgrade

Trek is getting a head start on the competition with the latest version of its Marlin+ electric mountain bike, becoming the first North American bicycle manufacturer to feature Bosch’s newly upgraded Active Line Plus motor.

The updated drive system brings more power, less weight, and a smaller footprint to Trek’s approachable electric mountain bike platform, helping make the Marlin+ 6 Gen 2 an even more compelling option for riders who want a capable e-bike without necessarily stepping up to a full-blown, high-performance electric mountain bike.

The Trek Marlin+ has traditionally occupied an interesting Goldilocks position in the company’s electric mountain bike lineup. It’s designed to offer the versatility of a trail-capable eMTB while remaining practical enough for everyday recreational riding, commuting, and exploring gravel paths.

In other words, it’s the kind of electric mountain bike that doesn’t require you to be an actual mountain biker to enjoy it.

And the new Bosch motor seems particularly well suited to that mission.

The biggest upgrade comes courtesy of Bosch’s new-generation Active Line Plus motor, which now offers up to 600 watts of power and 60 Nm of torque.

That’s paired with up to 340% pedal assistance, giving riders a substantial boost when accelerating or tackling climbs.

Despite the improved performance, Bosch has actually managed to shrink the motor. A redesigned two-stage gearbox reduces its volume by 17% while shaving approximately 1.1 lb (0.5 kg) from the previous generation.

The new motor weighs just around 6 lb (2.7 kg), helping manufacturers like Trek build lighter, more streamlined electric bicycles.

Bosch has also focused on improving the riding experience, with updated sensors and software designed to provide smoother, more natural-feeling assistance. Specially machined gears help make the motor virtually silent, while improved sealing and bearings are designed to withstand riding in all weather conditions.

The motor provides pedal assistance up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in the US, making it a Class 1 e-bike without a throttle. With a launch price of US $2,999, it’s also one of the more affordable options in Trek’s lineup.

For a bike like the Marlin+, that combination of moderate weight, smooth assistance, and plenty of usable power could be more important than chasing the enormous torque figures found on increasingly powerful premium eMTBs.

The new motor isn’t the only addition to Bosch’s electric bicycle ecosystem this fall.

The company has also unveiled its new Intuvia 200 display, featuring a 2.4-inch grayscale screen designed to remain readable in bright sunlight. It’s joined by a redesigned LED Controller that’s approximately 65% smaller than the previous LED Remote, offering five thumb-operated buttons and a USB-C charging port.

Bosch is also expanding its theft protection technology with an updated ConnectModule that uses Bluetooth Low Energy alongside GPS and cellular connectivity to help locate stolen e-bikes within a few yards, including in areas where GPS reception is poor.

Perhaps most interesting for long-distance riders is the new PowerTube 720 battery, which packs 720 Wh of capacity into a compact package weighing just 8.6 lb (3.9 kg). Bosch claims up to 115 miles (185 km) of range under favorable conditions on compatible touring e-bikes.

Those additional products are part of Bosch’s broader smart system updates, though Trek hasn’t confirmed which, if any, will be included on the updated Marlin+.

With Bosch supplying drive systems to a large number of e-bike makers worldwide, these upgrades will likely find their way onto plenty of other electric bicycles in the coming months.

But for now, Trek gets the distinction of being first in North America to bring the new Active Line Plus motor to riders.

#4655. 9 nature-inspired pumpkin carving patterns from the National Park Service

The approaching All Hallows Eve means the time has come to carve that jack-o’-lantern to light the way for trick-or-treaters or keep the bad spirits away. The National Park Service’s Pumpkin Carving Challenge offers gourd enthusiasts a way to celebrate nature’s spooky side.

“Nothing says ‘scary’ quite like a 2,000-pound furry mammal you’ve annoyed launching you into another dimension. Or the tree above. Either way, it comes with a thud. Talk about a smashing Halloween,” the NPS writes.

Carvers can choose from nine templates that can be used to craft a more off-the-beaten-path jack o’lantern. Templates include pictures of bats, spooky spiderwebs, and (our favorite), fat bears.

The Batty One celebrates one of Halloween’s most enduring symbols. National parks serve as  roosting grounds or migratory stops for millions of bats all year round, not just during spooky season.

The Close Encounter offers a cautionary tale. Please view animals from a safe distance for their safety and yours. One visitor to Yellowstone National Park certainly learned that in July.

The Autumn Leaves pays tribute to the spectacular display of color trees shown during the fall. And what could be more autumnal than leaf peeping in a national park?

The Full Moon is a template that will “eclipse” the others, according to the NPS. Wolves currently roam in at least six national parks.

The Camper is for those of us who love a good ghost story around a cracking camp fire.

The Fat Bear. Need we say more? Bring the Fat Bear Week fun right into Halloween with this template.

The Web Designer honors nature’s web slingers. The NPS even offers helpful tips on how to avoid the horror of walking into a spider web.

Pictures can be added to a growing digital pumpkin patch on social media using #FindYourPark or #EncuentraTuParque.

Some other ways to spice up your pumpkin creations this year include oozing pumpkins, using a vape to create a spooky smoke effect, and using kelp to make kelp-o’-lanterns.

#4654. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4653. BYD (BYDDY) Q3 profit jumps 28% on exports, but inventory balloons 60%

BYD’s Q3 2026 earnings are out, and net profit jumped 28% year-over-year to ¥10.02 billion as the Chinese automaker shipped more than half a million vehicles out of the country in just three months.

But the rest of the filing is messier. BYD’s inventory is up 60% since January, its cash pile has shrunk by almost half, and profit is still down for the first nine months of the year.

BYD is still operating at a high level, but its business is changing.

BYD filed its third-quarter report with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on Thursday. Here are the key figures for July through September:

That’s BYD’s best quarterly profit since the end of 2024, and the first time revenue has grown year-over-year after four straight quarters of declines.

It’s also a big rebound from the start of the year. BYD’s Q1 2026 profit collapsed 55% to ¥4.08 billion, before recovering to ¥8.24 billion in Q2.

Still, it came in under expectations. Brokerages polled by Reuters were looking for ¥11.4 billion to ¥12.95 billion.

And zoom out to the full year so far, and BYD is treading water. Revenue for the first nine months was ¥566.30 billion, up just 0.01%, while net profit fell 4.2% to ¥22.34 billion. That’s on top of 2025, when BYD’s annual profit had already dropped to ¥32.62 billion from ¥40.25 billion in 2024.

The quarterly report doesn’t break out vehicle volumes, but BYD’s monthly sales filings do. The automaker sold 1,323,065 vehicles in Q3, up 18.7% from 1,114,192 a year earlier.

All of that growth, and then some, came from outside China. BYD exported 550,704 vehicles in the quarter, up 137% from 232,806 in Q3 2025. Everything else, which is mostly the Chinese market, fell about 12% to roughly 772,000 units.

Exports now account for 42% of BYD’s sales. In the first half, overseas markets already brought in ¥181.3 billion, or 53% of the company’s revenue.

For perspective, Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles worldwide in Q3. BYD exported more cars than Tesla sold on the entire planet.

At home, it’s a different story. China’s price war hasn’t let up, and BYD is now fighting it with cars like the new Seagull with 5-minute flash charging, starting under $10,000. That’s great for buyers. Not so much for margins.

BYD doesn’t report gross margin in its quarterly filing, but it can be calculated from the income statement. We get about 18.0% for Q3, slightly better than 17.6% a year ago, but down from roughly 18.9% in Q2.

The bigger hits are further down the income statement.

Finance expenses came in at ¥7.37 billion for the first nine months, compared to a ¥2.94 billion gain in the same period last year. BYD blames exchange losses. That’s a swing of more than ¥10 billion when the company made ¥22.34 billion in profit, which is the price of doing half your business in foreign currencies.

Impairment charges are also climbing. BYD booked ¥2.71 billion in asset impairment losses, up 68%, which it says is mostly inventory write-downs because of “the expanded inventory scale.” Credit losses tripled to ¥944 million, set aside “in line with the increase in trade receivables.”

And then there’s R&D. BYD’s research and development expenses fell 17% to ¥36.28 billion over nine months. A small part of that is accounting, since BYD capitalized more development costs on its balance sheet this year, but it’s still a notable drop for a company that has built its brand on vertical integration and in-house tech.

Here’s how a few key line items moved between Dec. 31, 2025 and Sept. 30, 2026:

BYD attributes both the inventory and receivables jumps “mainly” to the growth of its overseas auto business. That makes sense. Cars on ships, in ports and at foreign dealers sit on the books a lot longer than a car sold to a dealer in China.

The bills payable number stands out too. Those are short-term notes BYD hands suppliers instead of cash, and they more than tripled this year, which BYD explains as “the increase in settlement of bills.”

On the financing side, BYD cut its short-term bank borrowings roughly in half to ¥18.67 billion, but tripled its bonds outstanding to ¥14.99 billion and issued super short-term commercial paper.

To be fair, there are healthy signals in there as well. Operating cash flow for the first nine months was ¥54.47 billion, up 33%. Customer prepayments (contract liabilities) rose 81% to ¥92.95 billion, which points to strong orders. And cash spent on new factories and equipment fell 24% to ¥87.38 billion as BYD’s huge buildout slows down.

On the surface, this is a good quarter for BYD. Profit is up 28%, revenue is growing again, and the export strategy is clearly working. BYD exporting more cars in a quarter than Tesla sells worldwide would have sounded absurd just three years ago.

But we don’t think it’s as clean as the headline number suggests.

BYD had a rocket like ascension and sales exploded while they kept on introducing better technology. Considering the competition increase, they are still doing very well. They are not even everywhere yet but that is probably coming at some point soon too.

BYD added over ¥83 billion worth of inventory in nine months while its sales were down 3.9% year-to-date. Receivables are up, supplier IOUs are up, and cash is way down. That’s what it looks like when you push a lot of cars into a long overseas pipeline and wait to get paid for them. It works as long as those cars sell at decent prices. If they don’t, those impairment charges we’re already seeing get a lot bigger.

And the domestic business isn’t getting easier. BYD is selling fewer cars in China than a year ago while it now employs over 1 million people. The cuts to R&D spending are a sign the company is looking for savings somewhere.

These are all signs of BYD’s business changing. It is going to take a while for it to settle, but I think they are currently in a great spot with the switch to their Blade battery 2.0 virtually over, and new capacity coming from Hungary, Thailand, and Brazil.
