SD: It’s a chocolate-like coating that can use vegetable fats in place of some of the cocoa butter you’d find in traditional chocolate, and those substitutions can make a difference in how a candy tastes and feels in your mouth.

LB: The phrase chocolate-like kind of raises a red flag there.

LB: Okay, but here’s the really important question. Did they actually change Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups?

SD: According to Hershey, no. The company says the original Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup recipe hasn’t changed, but it acknowledges that some other Reese’s products, different shapes and sizes and newer varieties, can have different formulations.

LB: Oh, so the classic peanut butter cup shape might be the same, but the other Reese’s candies, like the popular pumpkins or Christmas tree shapes, aren’t necessarily made the same way.

SD: Yes, at least that’s the distinction the company is making. But this isn’t just about Reese’s. Candy companies have been adjusting their recipes for years, and to understand why, Popular Science spoke with Dr. Richard Hartel, a food scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and he explained that one of the biggest reasons companies change their recipes is pretty straightforward: money.

SD: Yep. Candy manufacturers are a business, and when the price of ingredients goes up, they have a pretty strong incentive to find cheaper alternatives.

But those substitutions aren’t always obvious. Take caramel, for example.

SD: Yes, same. So traditionally, caramel might be made using whole milk and milk fat. But a manufacturer could decide to replace those ingredients with skim milk and a different kind of fat, like vegetable oil or coconut oil.

They might also replace some milk proteins with whey proteins.

SD: Potentially, but it can also change the flavor and texture of the final candy. Because even if two ingredients serve a similar purpose in a recipe, that doesn’t mean they’re gonna taste exactly the same.

LB: Right, and I imagine butter and vegetable oil don’t produce exactly the same caramel just because of chemistry.

You know, it’s like vegan or regular cooking. It’s similar, but different.

SD: Yeah. No, exactly. And the same thing can happen with chocolate. A company might reduce the amount of cocoa in a product while still keeping enough to meet the legal requirement for calling it “chocolate.”

LB: So there are legal requirements for calling it chocolate, kind of like with beer?

SD: There are, yeah. The FDA has what’s called standards of identity for certain foods. Basically, these are rules that determine what ingredients a product needs to contain or how it needs to be made to legally use a particular name. So you can’t necessarily just throw some brown colored sugar and oil together and call it milk chocolate.

LB: So it’s kind of similar to that question of if almond milk can really be called “milk.” Yes. Yeah, I guess it is kind of assuring that there are some sort of standards here.

SD: Oh, yeah. No, those standards still leave manufacturers, though, room to adjust the recipes. And if a company changes its ingredients while staying within those legal requirements, it generally doesn’t have to make some big public announcement or even change their ingredient list.

LB: Right, so there’s not gonna be a big press release saying, “Attention candy lovers, we’ve slightly reduced the cocoa content of your favorite chocolate bar.”

SD: Exactly, and that’s part of what makes this whole thing so sneaky. Because according to Hartel, some of these recipe changes are so subtle that even trained testers might not notice them.

LB: Really? So like even those lucky people whose job it is to literally taste things?

SD: Yep. Imagine you have a candy bar, you know, you’ve eaten your whole life. One year the company makes a tiny adjustment to the recipe. You probably don’t notice. The next year they make another tiny adjustment. Again, you probably don’t notice.

But if you keep doing that over 10 years or 20 years…

LB: Okay, so that explains why a candy bar might taste different now. But here’s what I’m wondering. If people notice these changes and don’t like them, why don’t companies just go back to the original recipes?

SD: Yeah, well that brings us to one of the most famous disasters in the history of food marketing: New Coke.

SD: So back in 1985, Coca-Cola decided to change its signature soda formula, and the company had actually done taste testing beforehand. In blind taste tests, people often preferred sweeter Pepsi over Coke. So Coca-Cola introduced a new sweeter version of its drink.

LB: Which as we now know, people famously hated.

SD: Hated it. And it’s all because of something called the Pepsi paradox. Basically, there’s a difference between tasting a tiny sip of something and actually consuming an entire serving. A sweeter drink might win in a quick sip test, but that doesn’t necessarily mean people want to drink a whole can.

LB: Right. That makes sense. Like if one bite of something is super sweet, it might be delicious—

LB: —but after 10 bites you might be completely over it.

SD: Yeah, and that’s a big challenge for food companies because just because a new recipe performs well in a taste test doesn’t mean consumers will actually prefer it in their everyday lives.

And with New Coke there was another huge factor.

LB: Okay. If it’s not money, I’m gonna guess it’s nostalgia.

SD: Nostalgia. People were attached to the original Coca-Cola. It wasn’t just about how the soda tasted. It was about the memories and feelings associated with it.

LB: All right, and that brings us right back to Halloween candy.

SD: Yeah. When you eat a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup or a Hershey’s bar, you’re not necessarily just tasting chocolate and sugar and peanut butter.

LB: You might also be remembering the fun of trick-or-treating as a kid, dumping your candy all over the living room floor and trading with your siblings.

SD: Or in my case, hiding an entire year’s supply of candy under my bed.

LB: Hey, I now think it’s very important to have a secret candy bunker.

SD: Look, I concur. And that brings us to another important part of this mystery because even if a candy company hasn’t changed its recipe at all, there’s still something else that could be changing.

SD: Us. Our sense of taste isn’t necessarily the same throughout our lives.

As we get older, our ability to perceive flavors can change, and one reason is that our taste buds don’t regenerate quite as quickly as they used to.

LB: So even if I’m eating a Milky Way, I might experience it differently now.

SD: Right, even if it’s the same exact Milky Way. And it’s not just aging. Our environment and experiences also affect how we perceive taste.

So the way you experience a Milky Way today might be different from the way you experienced it as a kid, even if the recipe is identical.

LB: Okay, so with this mystery, we’ve now got two possible culprits: the candy companies are changing the recipes, and our taste buds are changing too.

SD: And both things can be true at the same time, which makes it difficult to know whether your beloved Milky Way or addictive Nerds actually taste different or whether you just remember it tasting different.

LB: So basically, no matter how much we want to, we’re never getting that exact childhood Halloween candy experience back, no matter how much we try.

SD: I know, but there’s a little good news. Candy companies do sometimes listen when people complain about changes. In fact, Hershey has announced plans to bring back older recipes for some of its products, including certain miniature Easter candies.

LB: Okay, that helps. So there’s some hope.

SD: There is, but Hershey will still experiment with new formulas for other products, so I wouldn’t expect every candy to suddenly taste exactly the way it did in 1998.

SD: But here’s the big takeaway. If you’ve bitten into your favorite childhood candy and thought, “This isn’t as good as it used to be,” you might actually be onto something.

Manufacturers really do change the recipes. Sometimes those changes are tiny, and sometimes they accumulate over decades, but our own taste perception changes too. So the answer to whether candy tastes different now is—

SD: It really is. But before we wrap up this very sweet episode, there’s one thing I want to get to the bottom of because we spent this whole episode talking about how our favorite childhood candies might be changing, but what would someone who tastes food for a living think?

LB: I feel like we need to bring in the expert here.

SD: Me too, and luckily, we got a pretty great one. After the break, we’re gonna be joined by Jack Bishop from America’s Test Kitchen.

LB: Excellent. Love America’s Test Kitchen.

And we’re back with Jack Bishop. Jack is the senior content advisor at America’s Test Kitchen, where he’s been part of the team since the very beginning, starting with the launch of Cook’s Illustrated in 1993. He’s also the tasting lab expert on America’s Test Kitchen and Cook’s Country, which means he’s spent decades putting food to the test.

Jack, thank you so much for joining us on Popular Science’s Ask Us Anything podcast.

Jack Bishop: It’s great to be here, Sarah. Thanks for asking me.

SD: Oh, we’re so excited to have you. So Jack, throughout today’s episode, we’ve been investigating whether our favorite childhood candies really taste different than they used to, and I want to start with a personal question.

Was there a candy you absolutely loved growing up that just doesn’t quite taste as good to you today?

JB: —that’s pretty much true for most candies, especially I was a child of the ’60s and ’70s, and so candies were bigger back then. In my mind, the biggest difference is the caramel isn’t as gooey as it used to be when I was a kid.

JB: When you would bite into a Snickers bar, it was almost like a cheese pull. You know, you’d get this great pull, and I feel like that doesn’t happen anymore.

SD: And given your knowledge of food generally, why do you think Snickers taste different?

JB: You know, it’s hard to say because you do the label reading, and it only gets you so far.

JB: —you know, you can tell by the order of the ingredients. If that changes, that could be a real sign. You know, if something has gone up in the ingredient list, that likely means there’s more of it, because ingredients are listed in the order of sort of weight. You know, they’re just using lower quality ingredients in order to keep costs down.

I mean, that’s the overall trend in what I would call supermarket candy.

JB: Is cost is such a big issue, and so many of the inputs have gotten so expensive. And so, you know, using less of the expensive ingredient, switching out, you know, a moderately priced ingredient for a really cheap ingredient. Those are all strategies that could be used to control cost, but they’re not necessarily gonna make something tastier.

SD: Yeah. Yeah, and if, you know, a listener is listening to this and they feel like one of their favorite candies has changed since they were growing up, what would you suggest? How would they go about testing that?

JB: I should start by saying I think taste memories are powerful but unreliable.

JB: So what I mean by that is I can make a certain recipe, and the house fills with an aroma, like I’m thinking of like my grandmother’s lasagna, and if like my brother or sister walks in, it’s like we’re back in my grandmother’s kitchen, and, you know, I’m eight, and my sister’s seven, and my brother’s five again. The food is really triggering powerful emotions.

JB: But, you know, we misremember stuff, and it’s really hard to remember, well, how sweet was this?

JB: Right? How chocolatey was this? Was this really peanut buttery, or have my tastes just changed? And I know for me, you know, I now like 85 percent cacao chocolate.

Well, I didn’t like that as a kid. And so that will color perceptions of things I did eat when I was a kid, and is it not as good as it used to be, or do I not like that anymore? Unless you can get a time machine and somebody can send you a candy bar from, you know, 1972 or whatever year you’d like to go back to, you’re relying on your memory, and your memory’s a little fickle when it comes to food.

SD: Yeah, and we’ve actually been talking a bit in this episode about Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups because they’ve been at the center of this whole conversation about changing candy recipes, and I know America’s Test Kitchen actually has its own recipe for homemade peanut butter cups. So I’m curious, what makes a really great peanut butter cup? Is there something the homemade version can get right that a store-bought candy might not?

JB: Fewer ingredients and better ingredients. So, you know, if you read the label on a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup, it’s a pretty long ingredient list. Our homemade version starts with milk chocolate and creamy peanut butter that you enrich with a little bit of butter, a little bit of salt, and a little bit of confectioner sugar ‘cause the confectioner sugar will incorporate into the sugar without giving you any sort of grittiness, and that’s it.

It’s really just creamy peanut butter that’s a little sweeter and a little saltier and a little richer than it is straight out of the jar layered with melted chocolate, and you need, don’t need to anything more than put the chocolate in the microwave, 50 percent power to gently melt it, and then you can actually build them.

The easiest way to do this is in a mini muffin tin.

JB: And you can get little liners, and you sort of pipe a layer of chocolate, pipe a layer of peanut butter, and then finish with a layer of chocolate. So the chocolate’s not completely enrobing the peanut butter, but it’s the neatest, easiest way to do it at home, and it eats like…

Well, I won’t say it eats like a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup ‘cause it’s so much better.

SD: Well, Jack, thank you so much for joining us. I need to go make peanut butter cups apparently. And Jack, if listeners wanna know more about what you’re up to in America’s Test Kitchen, where should they go?

JB: Sure. We’ve got, you know, tastings of milk chocolate, dark chocolate, white chocolate, and you can find all of those results at americastestkitchen.com.

SD: Great. Thank you so much for making the time, Jack.

LB: Wow, I love him so much. And even though I can’t cook to save my life, I kind of want to try that homemade peanut butter cup recipe.

SD: I know, me too. We’ll link it in the show notes.

And if you like our show, leave us a rating and a review.

SD: What’s your favorite candy? Let us know in the comments. Our producer is Alan Haburchak, and this week’s episode was based on an article written for Popular Science by Andrew Coletti.

LB: Thank you, team, thank you, candy, and thank you everyone for listening.

SD: And one more time, if you want something you’ve always wondered about explained on a future episode, go to popsci.com/ask and click the “Ask Us” link. Until next time, keep the questions coming, and may your candy stay mice-free.

LB: I’m still sad about Baby Sarah’s candy stash.

#4614. Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.

But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?

One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.

He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.

That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.

But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.

Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.

The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.

By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.

Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.

Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.

Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.

And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.

Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.

Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”

Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.

That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.

The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.

Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.

Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.

When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”

There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.

Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.

Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.

Much like modern EVs, I would imagine a lot of these issues will be fixed via a software update. Early adoption is fun but you’re basically beta testing a product for the company at full price.

That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit. “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”

But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.

A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel.

And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.

#4613. Toyota Making the Land Cruiser's Cool Round Headlights Available After Purchase, But There's a Catch

J250 drivers can swap out their stock rectangular lights for the retro circular ones ... if they live in Japan.

The Toyota Land Cruiser has long been an enthusiast favorite, but the modern iteration arguably lacks some of its original charm—or at least, the amount it has might depend on what version you get and where you live. When the J250-generation Land Cruiser launched a few years back, Toyota linked its styling cues to trim level here in the United States Upscale trim Land Cruisers featured square headlights, while the base model Land Cruiser 1958 trim (as well as the First Edition) had rounded headlights. However, the 250 Series Land Cruiser only came with square headlights in many overseas markets.

Now, Toyota will offer a round headlight retrofit as an option on all 250-Series Land Cruisers. There is, however, a catch: at least for now, the add-on is only available in the Japanese market.

The replacement parts feature a taller lighting unit with circular LED daytime running lights with the Land Cruiser logo and larger amber indicators at the side. This helps fill front-end space, and aligns the light with the bottom edge of the grille. The new round headlight option will be available on Land Cruisers produced after April 2024 for ¥204,600, or $1296 at current exchange rates; his pricing includes installation.

And the round headlight design isn’t just cooler; it actually works better. Insurance Institute for Highway Safety testing revealed that the round design provides superior visibility compared to the squared-off design. Toyota Land Cruiser 1958 models earned a "good" rating with their round headlights, while Land Cruisers with square headlights only managed a “marginal" rating. Here’s hoping Toyota begins offering the after-market headlight upgrade here in the States, too.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4612. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

#4611. World War II’s baby gas masks are as unnerving as you’d imagine

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:54 AM EDT

Time forgets the vast majority of inventions—usually for good reason. As parents and children everywhere get ready for trick-or-treating, we’d like to turn your attention to one such invention: the baby gas mask.

In the November 1938 issue of Popular Science, “a doll demonstrates the use of the baby gas mask” in an undeniably creepy image. The word mask is perhaps a misnomer here, because this contraption actually completely engulfs the baby as “filtered air is pumped in with an artificial lung.”

These baby gas masks were developed at a time when around the world people feared another world war would—and eventually did—ignite. The brief story on the contraption reads, “Babies are protected from poison gas in case of a wartime attack” by these novel masks.

But it’s still hard to imagine any baby well-behaved enough to sit inside such a creepy invention. Nonetheless, the French inventors behind the technology thought this would be a good idea—even a profitable one. And in the lead up to World War II, the baby gas mask briefly caught on, with several vintage photographs showing off different iterations of the device.

In one 1937 image (featured above), a woman and young toddler both sport gas masks in Germany.

There’s also a whole slew of children and babies wearing gas masks in vintage photographs from England. One photograph (below) shows how a baby gas mask, also known as a hood, worked as a woman demonstrates using the contraption at the historic Holborn Town Hall in London, England.

This particular design took three years to develop. An infant is placed inside a fabric hood featuring a large cellulose acetate window. A drawstring cinches the hood at the infant’s waist, so that the arms, shoulders, and head are completely contained. An adult then operates a rubber bellows to filter air into the hood.

There was apparently no time limit for how long a child could be kept inside the airtight mask—as long as air was steadily pumped in, of course. As to whether the infant enjoyed the contraption, no one could ask.

Another photograph taken (fittingly) during Halloween season, on October 20, 1937, at Dr. Barnardo’s nursery home in Hawkhurst, Kent, England, shows several toddlers in a more traditional face gas mask. The home was actually nicknamed the Babies’ Castle. It originally opened in 1883, after a Mr. Theodore Moillet donated two adjacent mansions and an acre of meadowland for the nursery.

Yet another photograph from England shows several mothers holding babies fitted with the hood-style gas mask designed by the Royal Air Force.

Hospitals in England were also fitted with baby gas masks, and one 1940 photograph shows several nurses testing out the new technology.

One little girl named Jean Panter even convinced her father to make her doll a gas mask. This photograph of little Jean with her doll was taken in England on February 11, 1938, shortly before World War II began. The fact that even a young girl wanted a gas mask for her beloved toy certainly speaks to how much fears of poison gas permeated society before and during World War II.

In 1938, Dr. Jacques Marie Le Mée (sometimes spelled La Mee or Le-Mee), the head physician at the Hôpital Necker-Enfants-Malades in Paris, developed another type of baby gas mask. In fact, the hospital Le Mée worked at is the oldest children’s hospital in the Western world, initially founded in 1801 as Hôpital des Enfants Malades.

In one 1939 photograph, several women and their babies don Le Mée’s baby gas mask in a Parisian square. As opposed to the baby gas hoods on display in vintage English photographs, Le Mée’s invention envelopes the entire baby’s body. Even the baby’s legs will get clean air.

Even though the November 1938 issue of Popular Science says the baby gas mask gracing its pages was developed in France, it’s markedly different to the above photograph of Le Mée’s baby gas mask.

In this design, the window is larger and it’s also unclear how the baby gas mask cinches or becomes airtight around the infant.

Someone holding the child pumps fresh air into the hood-style gas mask. “The person holding the infant controls the amount of fresh air entering the [baby] shelter by pressing on the rubber-lung unit,” the short story in the magazine reads.

But even in dark times, children always find a way to have fun. In one delightful comment on a BBC story about baby gas masks, one reader, William Irwin, remembers having “endless fun playing ‘divers’ with one” baby gas mask.

“We were so far removed from bombing risk areas so I do not believe I was ever put into it as a war-baby. It gave me the interest to eventually become a scuba sports diver.”

Even though this technology thankfully fell by the wayside and seems very strange to modern eyes, it still offers us a lot to think about. The inventions that come out of hard times can even inspire—at least if you’re William Irwin.

In That Time When, Popular Science tells the weirdest, most surprising, and little-known stories that shaped science, engineering, and innovation.

#4609. Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive

Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker LiveWire has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.

The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.

LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.

The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.

The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.

The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.

The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.

LiveWire is also preparing to showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.

Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.

This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.

Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.

Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle well over a decade ago and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.

Maybe it's news to Electrek, but while Harley was contemplating electric motorcycles, Zero was selling them for over a decade and continues to do so. There are some high end bikes that Livewire just didn't compete with yet cost $30k when it first came out damaging the brand perception. Newer, lower priced models don't help.

There is also competition from run around eScooters that are way cheaper even cheaper than upcoming Honcho.

And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.

The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.

In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.

I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

#4608. Mate Rimac’s Bugatti Chiron Was Stolen From the Factory After He Left the Keys Inside

The car was quickly tracked down, and the CEO now says he’ll stop leaving his keys inside his multi-million dollar hypercar.

Mate Rimac, by just about any definition, is a very smart man. After all, this is a man who arguably revolutionized the electric car as much as that fellow from South Africa who gets all the press; a man who created his own EV racer as a teenager, his own electric hypercar company before he was 22 years old, and explored the bleeding edge of high-end EVs so impressively that Porsche and the VW Group gave him the reins of Bugatti at the age of 33. (He is also a very polite, patient, and fun man, as I found while interviewing him at the Geneva Motor Show and he was game to do a Vanna White impression for camera to show off the Rimac Nevera.)

But we all have blind spots. One of his, apparently, involves occasionally leaving the keys to his own personal Bugatti Chiron in the car—and on Wednesday, that led to the in-hindsight-perhaps-obvious occurrence of someone stealing his multi-million dollar speed machine from the Rimac factory.

Rimac spilled the beans himself in a set of social media posts on Thursday, explaining exactly what happened. Croatia, he stresses, is a very safe place, so for years now, he’s been leaving his keys in his cars, be they his Nevera or his Chiron or whatever else. But while the buildings are secured, the compound is fairly open, which the CEO says enabled a stranger to wander in and take the car.

After some brief confusion as to whether someone authorized to take the car had borrowed it, Rimac says, he and his crew realized the Bugatti had been boosted, and called the police. As officers arrived, Rimac says he was tracking the Chiron from its on-board telemetry, and realized it was heading towards the Slovenian border. So, being awesome, the CEO gave chase in the Porsche 911 he happened to have on hand.

Rimac says the driver made it all the way to Austria before authorities there, aided by real-time updates from the factory, were able to stop the Bugatti. At the police station there, the CEO says the thief claimed he had actually come to the factory looking for a job, then saw the Chiron with the key inside— “Like it was my fault!”, Rimac says with astonishment—and then took off with the car. (Rimac says the man was planning to go to Germany “for whatever reason,” but I think we can all make a guess as to why.)

The second, perhaps even more dramatic post, showcased the security camera footage of the theft itself. In it, the apparently cigarette-smoking thief ever-so-slowly sidles up to the blue Bugatti, glancing around before eventually taking one final drag and clambering into the car. The CEO wisely went for “The Pink Panther Theme” as a soundtrack here, but the Parks & Recreation “Don’t Be Suspicious” song would work just as well.

Suffice it to say, Rimac says he will not be keeping the keys in the cars from now on. “Don’t try your luck—it will not happen again,” he says.

#4607. Seven young condors released in northern California

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:12 AM EDT

In 1986, there wasn’t a single California condor (Gymnogyps californianus) left in the wild. Thankfully, it wasn’t because the birds of prey had gone extinct, but they were getting close. In the 1980s, there were fewer than two dozen condors remaining in the wild. That’s why the United States Fish and Wildlife Service moved them into a captive breeding and release program.

Now, the Northern California Condor Restoration Program has released seven young condors into the wild in Yurok Country, close to the Oregon border, according to a statement emailed to Popular Science. One of the birds is particularly special—the condor represents the 200th California condor hatched at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park to be released into the wild. In total, the safari park has hatched 291 condors since 1982.

The seven recently released condors will join 26 other condors already enjoying the Yurok Country site. It’s the most recently established California condor release site, and received its first released condors in 2022. The NCCRP is a collaboration between the Yurok Tribe and the Redwood National and State Parks.

“Condor releases are critical to achieving our ultimate goal- to reestablish a self-sustaining condor population in the wild,” Joe Burnett, California Condor Recovery Program Manager at the Ventana Wildlife Society in California, previously told Popular Science.

It was Burnett that taught us about an unexpected behavior in young condors: the “zoomies” we more frequently associate with dogs.

“We observe the zoomies in both captive and wild condors. It’s just a sudden expression of pure excitement for young condors and very fun to watch,” Burnett explained at the time. “They just can’t contain themselves and totally let loose. They hop, run in circles, or flap around, or all the above! It’s just pure fun!”

It’s unclear whether the special “200th” bird experienced such a display. Either way, the release is happy news. There are now seven more condors in the wild, when only a few years ago there were none.

#4606. Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these new reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

She said issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” said Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are important windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” said William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” said Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they said could reverse these trends. Among them:

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu said.

Weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan said women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”

#4605. Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.

The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.

So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.

This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.

That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.

OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.

Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.

I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.

Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.

Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

The Poki is currently priced at $1,799, and customers can get 5% off with the code Electrek.

#4604. Tested: 2027 BMW M350 xDrive Is Fast But Not Furious

Behind the Neue Klasse design, the eighth-generation 3-series gets the basics right.

The BMW 3-series is no longer the company’s best-selling car in the United States, but it is still the model closest to the formula that earned the brand its success and status with American enthusiasts. The all-new G50 is the eighth generation of 3-series and will be reaching the U.S. next year, with buyers initially able to choose between a four-cylinder 330 and an inline-six-powered M350 xDrive. It’s the latter, in European specification, that’s being tested here. Is this still the heart of the BMW brand?

Another product of BMW’s Neue Klasse era, the new 3-series gets radical new styling that closely aligns it with the fully electric i3 that will be sold alongside it (which we test separately here). But don’t let the looks fool you—beneath the surface, the two cars sit on different architectures and have subtly different dimensions. The gasoline-powered version is fractionally shorter and sits on a 112.6-inch wheelbase, 1.5 inches less than the EV’s.

The new M350 effectively replaces the previous G20-generation M340i, using a version of BMW’s long-serving B58 turbocharged inline-six that works in conjunction with a 48-volt mild hybrid system. This makes 437 horsepower and 428 lb-ft of torque, increases of 55 hp and 59 lb-ft over the outgoing car.

Drive is delivered through an eight-speed automatic transmission and an xDrive-branded all-wheel system as standard. The option of rear-wheel drive is no longer available. BMW plans to offer a switchable rear-wheel drive mode, but this wasn’t on the car R&T tested in France, as the company plans to introduce it later though a software update.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Transmission: eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive

The presence of BMW’s famous M badge on any model still raises expectations, even knowing that the M350 xDrive is a member of the M Performance range, essentially a diffusion line that sits beneath the fully-fledged M cars that keep single digits. The fact it has more power and torque than the F80-generation M3, which was on sale as recently as 2018, increases anticipation further.

The good news is the new car absolutely delivers on raw performance. BMW claims a 3.9-second 0–60-mph time, one that is almost certain to be substantially bettered with the scientifically applied brutality of instrumented testing. And the car feels every bit as quick as that number suggests, launching with M-appropriate seriousness and with huge, linear urge that barely diminishes as speeds turn extra-legal. It sounds good too, with a snarling exhaust note that proved to be mostly organic even when I deactivated the switchable active noise enhancement, but which wasn’t intrusive or droning at cruising speeds.

At lower revs there is a hint of turbo lag, the hybrid system not bringing enough punch to cancel this out, but the quick-shifting gearbox means I had to hunt this down by using the transmission’s manual mode to keep revs low. But out of the box, it feels like a substantial performance upgrade over the outgoing G20-generation M340i.

All the horses and pounds of twist are delivered to the road with a minimum of drama. On my test route in the south of France, the M350 punched out of tight corners without a hint of slip, only the combination of big throttle openings with high cornering loads creating any sense that the majority of power was traveling to the rear wheels. The M350’s dynamic brain kept everything under tight control, and while the forthcoming Drift Moment mode will doubtless unlock a wilder side to the car’s character, but on dry, smooth asphalt the lateral-g loadings generated by the Bridgestone Potenza tires were high enough that I didn’t feel any urge to go and explore the limits of grip on a tight mountain road.

Of course, the presence of occasional, accessible drama has long been a core part of the appeal of punchier M-branded BMWs, and on first impressions, this definitely felt to be lacking. The different dynamic modes did change the M350’s demeanor, with Sport and Sport Plus adjusting throttle mapping and steering weight. But none turned it into a party animal. This is one of those cars that is all business. The combination of true excitement and a gasoline engine will likely require waiting for the forthcoming combustion G84 M3, which will ultimately sit alongside the EV version.

It’s been a long while since steering excellence came as standard on most BMW models. Although the M350’s slightly ovoid steering wheel delivered crisp, linear front-end responses, actual feedback was muted and only present at all once the firm hand of the active lane-keeping system was turned off. The car felt stable and impressively precise in faster corners, but at lower speeds, the assistance weighting was too soft for my tastes in all its switchable modes.

The gentler side of the M350’s personality earns unstinted praise. Ride quality has improved markedly over the M340i, with the new car’s adaptive dampers dealing with every road surface I could find to throw at them. Beyond the engine noise—which is definitely a plus—the cabin stayed impressively quiet for a sports sedan, one area where BMW had clearly transferred learning from its well-insulated EVs. And the Highway Assistant system, a hands-off Super Cruise–style enhanced cruise control, kept the car centered in its lane, reacted to other vehicles intelligently, and even executed lane changes in response to a turn signal input. I did only a few kilometers of high-speed French Autoroute, but it was enough to show the M350 will be a relaxed, high-speed cruiser.

While the combustion 3-series isn’t an EV, it has an EV’s interior. Barring minor details the cabin architecture is identical to that of the i3, and while that means an abundance of technology it has also brought compromises.

BMW’s new “Panoramic Vision” is front and center. Literally, the narrow projection band that sits between dashboard and windshield goes the whole width of the cabin, serving as an elongated gauge cluster. The shape of this showstopping display is not naturally suited to the needs of a combustion car, with a tiny fuel gauge all the way to one side and the M350’s rev counter being a narrow strip in front of the driver where two graphic bars move away from each other as the engine spins faster. This lacked the simple clarity of a conventional rev counter, and while it is possible to place a rendered tacho into one of the panoramic screen’s reconfigurable slots, the display’s lack of height means this was small and hard to see.

Other elements that can be added include images of some of BMW’s classic Art Cars and a rendered M badge. Which is cool but emphasizes how much more room is on the display than there strictly needs to be. Making full use of the commendable lowness of the new car’s seating position also meant the top of the rim obstructed the part of the Panoramic Vision display unless the wheel was adjust to be a little low.

The primary touchscreen is the same diagonal-edged 17.9-inch one that we’ve already seen in the iX3 and the new X5, this running the latest BMW X operating system. This generally worked well, making it pretty easy to find more commonly used functions, although with the need to go mining through submenus and scrollable pages to reach minor ones. There is a permanently rendered line of heating and ventilation controls at the base of this display, but the temperature controls are small and fiddly to operate. And, like the iX3, the angle of the new 3’s air vents need to be adjusted using the touchscreen, making something that should be simple needlessly complex.

Interior space has been improved compared with the previous generation, with ample head and shoulder room up front and plentiful seat adjustment, along with a more obvious upgrade in the back, where occupants enjoy more legroom. This isn’t a car many would choose for regularly transporting full-size adults over long distances, but a six-footer could sit behind another six-footer, with both in reasonable comfort. Trunk space is 11.3 cubic feet, only fractionally less than the Mercedes C-class.

The M350’s M badge also earns it the M Sport steering wheel rather than the strangely styled four-spoke wheel that will go into the regular car. This looks better but still has a heavily thickened rim on each side, which makes it look like a halfway-evolved yoke. It was a little unwieldy when making inputs requiring more than a turn of lock. Some hidebound traditionalists might prefer their steering wheels to be, you know, round.

The existence of a nearly visually identical BMW i3 asks the most obvious question for those considering the gasoline-powered version. In its basic 50 form, the EV is slightly less expensive—$62,850 to the M350 xDrive’s $67,250, both of those including destination. Admittedly, the forthcoming i3 M60 is probably the closer comparison, but BMW hasn’t released pricing for that one yet.

Direct combustion rivals are thin on the ground at the moment. The Audi S5 is no longer, technically, a sedan, and is down on power compared with the BMW. And we’re still waiting for details on how AMG is planning to replace the C43 in the freshly revised lineup.

But anybody arriving at M350 ownership directly from an M340i is going to feel like they have received a substantial upgrade, that delivered in terms of performance, technology and practicality. We will get used to BMW's radical new direction in time, and the basics are all solid.

A welcome return to the quad exhaust tailpipes that BMW lost by hiding the M340i’s exhaust within shaped finishers integrated into the bumper. Even a junior M car deserves to have its pipes standing loud and proud.

#4603. Male black bear ‘Nugget’ wins Introvert Award for his adorable hiding technique

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:48 AM EDT

Like the patient Paul, a male black bear (Ursus americanus) named Nugget would rather hang back alone than jump right into the salmon fest. For his solo tendencies, the team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded Nugget the 2026 Introvert Award.

“For much of the season, Nugget could be seen wedged between rocks by lower falls,” the U.S. Forest Service team writes. “If you saw a furry, black head with glassy eyes poking out of a crack—that’s Nugget! You could also find him perched on a rock waiting for his turn to fish in the lower falls hierarchy; afraid to assert his dominance in the crowd.”

Nugget was first spotted in the area only two years ago, and is beloved for his small size. He has a reddish coat that shifts to black later in the season. Nugget is often described as “scrappy.” He mostly scavenged during his first season at the creek, but slowly learned to catch salmon.

“The pristine ecosystem around Anan Creek allows even small, scrappy bears like Nugget to thrive,” the Rangers write.

The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest are currently doling out the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

The nation’s largest national forest, Tongass covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 known bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their chunky counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear and explore.org’s cameras also broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4601. Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, said Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she said.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he said. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

“It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy said.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy said. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive plan,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.
