#4565. Tested: 2027 BMW i3 50 xDrive Is in a Neue Klasse of Its Own

With strong performance and class-leading range, the sedan makes a compelling argument for going electric. But will potential buyers care?

First came the EVs that looked very obviously like electric cars, with wacky designs showing off their futuristic powertrains. Then there was a generation that hid EV powertrains under bodywork shared with combustion-powered models. And now we are encountering a new strain, EVs that look almost identical to regular siblings but sit on radically different underpinnings. And the BMW i3 is the best example yet of this new genre. From the outside, it looks almost indistinguishable from the gasoline-powered G50 3-series, but every exterior panel is different, and it sits on a completely different architecture, BMW’s Neue Klasse EV platform. The distinction is great enough that it even gets its own BMW model code—this is the NA0.

The Neue Klasse underpinnings mean the i3 shares its powertrain with the iX3 SUV that was launched ahead of it. The closeness of the relationship is shown by the 114.1-inch wheelbase shared by both models, primarily dictated by the use of the same battery pack.

The first version of the electric sedan to reach the U.S. will be the i3 50 xDrive, which uses a pair of electric motors, one powering each axle, to deliver a combined system output of 463 horsepower and 476 lb-ft of torque. The 800-volt battery stores 108.7 kWh of usable energy, and the i3’s lower profile and more slippery shape mean it will boast an EPA range of up to 468 miles. It also supports DC fast-charging at rates of up to 400 kW, making it theoretically possible to take the battery from a 10 percent to 80 percent state of charge in as little as 21 minutes. Providing you can hook it up to a sufficiently juicy plug, of course.

Other versions will follow, including an M60 version that will share the more potent powertrain of the iX3 M60 xDrive, making over 600 horsepower. Beyond that there is the fully electric M3 to look forward to, but for now we’ll concentrate on the meat-and-potatoes 50 xDrive.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Powertrain: dual electric motors, all-wheel drive

EPA Range: <468 miles (depending on wheels and tires)

Driving the i3 back-to-back with its 3-series doppelgänger, the new M350 xDrive, gave a fascinating insight into BMW’s priorities. Because it’s fair to say, when it comes to driving dynamics, that the EV has much more in common with the iX3 than it does with its combustion sibling. The M350 feels largely familiar, essentially a retuned and more powerful version of the previous-generation M340i xDrive. The i3 is breaking new ground for a BMW sedan. And yes, that comparison includes the old i4, which was—beneath its low-roofed bodywork—essentially an electric version of the last 3-series.

BMW has spent big on its Neue Klasse platform, and the i3 50 drove with a sense of oneness and harmony that proved the scale of the colossal engineering effort spent on integrating its different systems and making them play nice together. This was obvious in the smoothness of the powertrain, the poise of the chassis, and the exceptional refinement. This is clearly the new 3-branded model on which the big bucks have been spent.

Before I heap too much praise, I need to make an important proviso: The i3 50 is not, intrinsically, an exciting car. It is capable of delivering adrenaline spikes through quantities of longitudinal and lateral g-forces, but it completely lacks the rowdy character common to the BMWs that enthusiasts really love. Driving the i3 after experiencing the M350’s snarling engine and more aggressive suspension tune made the EV feel a little like a wallflower.

But that first impression was unfair. There’s a subtlety to the way the i3 50 does pretty much everything. No part of the experience really stands out, but that’s because everything is being done just so, and cruising refinement is almost spookily good. There is still a speaker-delivered soundtrack to try to introduce some excitement to proceedings, and it was too loud and intrusive in Sport mode. But this is switchable, and near silence suits the i3 much better.

By the increasingly deranged standards of the sharp end of the EV segment, performance is warm rather than outright hot: BMW claims a 4.5-second 0–60, which is actually 0.6 second slower than the M350. But it felt plenty keen behind the wheel, with the fractional difference in acceleration more than compensated for by not needing to change gears. Like the best EVs, the i3 has the ability to almost teleport itself into gaps and make passing moves at minimal notice. And while the rate of acceleration started to noticeably slacken over 85 mph, it still feels plenty rapid. Ultimately, BMW says, it will reach a 124-mph speed limiter.

Slowing impressed more than going, thanks to the completely seamless switching between regenerative and friction braking, the exceptionally finely tuned one-pedal mode, and also the Soft Stop feature—called “chauffeur stop” by other automakers—which brings the i3 to a genuinely imperceptible halt by easing braking progressively in the final few feet in its one-pedal mode. In addition to switchable regen levels, there is also an adaptive function that automatically increases this when the vehicle is approaching junctions or has other reasons to slow down, and it worked delicately enough to be hardly noticeable. The enhanced cruise control also worked well on different types of road, with the Highway Assistant function giving hands-off freeway functionality.

Most comments are exactly the same as those for the new 3-series. Despite their different underlying architectures, the 3-series and the i3 have what are almost identical cabins. The only obvious changes are that the EV doesn’t have gearchange paddles behind its steering wheel, a rev counter, or a start button; as long as the key is detected within the car, you just select a gear and go. Beyond that, the biggest difference I noticed was that the i3’s lowest seat position was higher than the M350’s, which was a mild frustration. Other comments regarding the sometimes fiddly inputs of the user interface are exactly the same for both cars.

The Neue Klasse cabin architecture was clearly designed with EVs higher on the priority list than combustion models. The Panoramic Vision projected dash display is better suited for delivering the minimal messages required the i3, losing the frustration of the M350’s inadequate rev counter and vestigial fuel gauge. There is still too much display real estate for the information that needs to be delivered, but the reconfigurable slots mean buyers will be able to make their own choices about what to look at, including images of some of BMW’s Art Cars.

I didn’t get the chance to test either the peak charging speed or the veracity of the impressive range claim. That will happen when Road & Track gets more time with a car in the States.

Potential buyers face two big questions. The first, if they are set on making the slightly eccentric choice of a compact EV sedan, is whether the i3 represents the best of the breed. Of the limited pool, the Mercedes C-class Electric, also set to reach the U.S. next year, is probably the closest alternative. But the Tesla Model 3 Performance is also a pretty close match in terms of power output, and it’s slightly less expensive, although it doesn’t get close to the BMW’s EPA range or dynamic polish.

But here’s a trickier question: Does this buyer really want an EV? For anyone determined to take the electric path, the i3 50 xDrive makes a great case for itself, one that will be strengthened as the model range fills out with other variants. But for those who prefer a more traditional take on the small BMW sedan or are sitting on the fence, the new 3-series provides what is still a compelling reason to say no. By empirical standards, the i3 is a better car, but it is not a more exciting one.

The chance to put pictures of some of BMW’s famous Art Cars onto the panoramic gauge cluster might feel like whimsy in a less serious car, but the i3 gets a pass given how relentlessly well it does pretty much everything else. As in other models with the new Panoramic Vision system, you can choose among five, including David Hockney’s superb BMW 850 CSi, seen here.

#4564. Speeders just got lucky: the new Chevy police Silverado is NOT electric

Say what you will about America’s police forces, but they are loyal – often to each other, and always to their preferred brand of pursuit vehicle. And if the thin blue line of Chevy faithful won’t embrace the 750 hp electric Silverado because it’s powered by batteries, that can really only be called a win for the scofflaws they’re pursuing.

A new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 9C1 police pursuit vehicle (PPV) was on display in the GM Fleet booth at the Orange County Convention Center this past week, where the new half-ton was featured fitted a new, 402 hp version of the venerable 5.7 small-block Chevy V8 sending 428 lb-ft of torque to both axles through a 10-speed automatic transmission. The 9C1 also features an available 2″ lift kit that retains the truck’s pursuit rating, up to 9,300 lbs. of towing capacity, and an available driver’s side LED spotlight.

If that all sounds somewhat pedestrian, it might be because Electrek readers are more familiar with the Silverado EV, which offers more than 750 hp in WOW mode and 775 lb-ft of torque at 0 rpm, along with a pessimistic EPA rating of just 478 miles – which, hilariously, is about the same “range” as the 16 mpg (combined) gas version, despite the EV packing nearly 350 additional horsepower, the ability to cruise in silence, and the significantly reduced maintenance and total cost of ownership costs of going electric.

Which, I guess, are all reasonably obvious things that nobody actually asked me about – and certainly nobody with a criminal justice degree and a statistically low LSAT score, so I’ll get back to talking about the truck, itself.

A massive, 16″ touchscreen display dominates the interior of the PPV, and was also touted as a standard feature (as it across Chevy’s civilian line), though if and how it would integrate with police department software isn’t clear – and my guess is that enforcement computing will continue to be an upfitter issue.

I don’t know why anyone would use a truck as a persuit vehicle? It seems reckless inefficient and ineffective.

Guess we are on the topic of us policing…

#4563. 2026 Gifts of the Year: Our editors have picked the best presents for anyone on your list

Updated Nov 1, 2026 3:42 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

A gift card isn’t a terrible present, but we believe you can do better. That’s why the editors here at Popular Science have put together this list of our favorite gifts of the year. We spend all year researching, testing, and covering products, so we know what we’re talking about. Even if you don’t end up grabbing one of these exact products, it’s a great place to start. Show them you know what they like and leave the gift cards for your nephew who you don’t really like that much.

Popular Science‘s sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at PCMag, CNET, Mashable, Lifehacker, and ZDNET.

Waterproof trail shoes usually look and feel too bulky and—let’s be honest—kind of nerdy. The Speedgoat 7 GTX keeps the regular Speedgoat 7’s supercritical EVA midsole and Vibram Megagrip outsole, then wraps them in a GORE-TEX Invisible Fit membrane and a recycled Cordura upper. It’s a lot of technical materials, but they’re wrapped in a design that actually looks cool with a pair of jeans. Toggle laces work with gloves on, there’s a loop for attaching gaiters (sold separately), and reflective details run all the way around for dark November runs. We recommend going up a half-size from your giftee’s typical number for a better fit.

This little device gives the gift of time that would otherwise be spent doomscrolling. Phone screen-time limits are easy to dismiss because the override button sits right under your thumb. Brick moves the override into another room. The $59 block has no battery, just an NFC chip. You pick the apps to lock in the free iPhone or Android app, tap your phone to the Brick, and those apps stay locked until you walk back and tap again. One Brick works with multiple phones, so a household can share it, and the app includes five emergency unlocks per device for real emergencies. It requires iOS 18 or Android 12 and later. Brick is also HSA and FSA eligible, which makes it a stocking stuffer you can buy with pretax money.

Insta360 made its name with 360-degree and action cameras, and the Luna Ultra is its first pocket gimbal camera, co-engineered with Leica. The main camera pairs a Leica Summicron lens with a 1-inch sensor that records up to 8K at 30fps, and a second telephoto camera on a 1/1.3-inch sensor handles zoomed shots and background blur. A three-axis gimbal keeps footage steady while you walk. The 2-inch OLED touchscreen pops off and works as a wireless monitor and remote, so you can frame a shot of yourself from across the room. It’s a serious content creation tool that’s fun to use, which is a rarity.

You don’t need a massive backyard to have a true outdoor pizza oven. The propane cooker weighs 26.4 pounds and measures 16.9 inches wide, yet Gozney rates it to reach 950 degrees Fahrenheit, which is more than enough to put a perfect char on a true Neopolitan style pie. Gozney’s lateral rolling flame wraps heat over the top of the pizza while a 12mm stone floor stores heat for the crust. An infrared thermometer makes a smart add-on gift, since the oven won’t tell you when the stone is ready. You’ll selfishly also probably get some free pizza out of it.

A 65-inch black rectangle is a lot of nothing to stare at when the TV is off. LG’s Gallery TV LX7B fills that space with art. The 4K Mini LED set has a matte screen that cuts reflections and a snow-white magnetic frame that snaps onto the bezel, and when it’s idle it can display pieces from LG Gallery+, a library of more than 5,000 works (some features require a Gallery+ subscription). It runs webOS 26 with Google Gemini built in. Whether the receiver is a film buff or a die-hard design enthusiast, this TV fits the bill.

This is a product we use every single day. The Theragun Mini Plus is Therabody’s smallest heated massage gun, and its attachment warms up to 131 degrees Fahrenheit across three heat levels. It has three speeds, two buttons, USB-C charging, and a travel lock that keeps it from switching on inside a gym bag. Therabody says heat plus percussion works three times faster than percussion alone, based on its own lab testing. You can run either therapy by itself, too. Don’t think this is only for hardcore gym rats. It’s great for people who just want to relax of even improve their sleep.

If you know a budding streamer or podcaster, this is a gift that grows with them. The Razer Seiren V3 Pro has both USB-C and XLR outputs, so it plugs straight into a PC now and into a mixer later when they upgrade their setup. It’s a dynamic mic with a 30mm cardioid capsule, a type that picks up less of a noisy room than most condensers. Onboard processing runs AI noise removal, a compressor, and a limiter on the mic itself, and Windows users can record 32-bit float audio through Razer Synapse. A tap-to-mute button, an RGB ring that shows mute and gain status, and an adjustable desk arm all come in the box.

The nightstand device, built for kids roughly 4 to 10, walks one child through morning, after-school, and bedtime routines a step at a time with visual prompts that work for kids who can’t read yet. It also handles alarm clock, sound machine, nightlight, and OK-to-wake duty. It has no camera or microphone, and kids can’t browse the web or download apps on it. Skylight sells it for $139.99, and the optional $39-per-year Buddy Plus plan adds rewards, timers, and read-aloud messages.

Fast wireless charging makes a magnetic battery pack hot, and heat makes phones slow their charging down. Anker’s fix in the MagGo 2 Pro is a tiny fan. The 10,000mAh pack charges at up to 25W over Qi2.2, and Anker says the fan keeps its back under about 97 degrees Fahrenheit while it works. Anker rates it to take an iPhone 17 Pro to 50 percent in about 25 minutes. A screen shows battery level and charging speed, a built-in stand props the phone up for in-flight movies, and the USB-C port refills the pack at 45W. It costs $109.99. Older phones, including the iPhone 15 Pro, top out at 15W.

Google hadn’t released a new standalone smart speaker since the Nest Audio in 2020. The Google Home Speaker is built around Gemini for Home instead of the old Assistant, so you can stack several requests into one sentence or correct yourself mid-command. It plays 360-degree sound from a 58mm driver, two of them pair with a Google TV Streamer for surround sound, and it doubles as a Thread border router and Matter hub. It costs $99.99 and includes six months of Google Home Premium, which adds Gemini Live and continued conversation. After the trial, Premium runs $10 per month.

A $20 smart plug makes a surprisingly good energy audit. The Shelly Plug Gen4 measures real-time power draw from whatever is plugged into it, so you can see how much that garage fridge or space heater actually pulls. It connects over Matter, Wi-Fi, or Zigbee, works with Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings, and Home Assistant, and can run locally without touching the cloud. It handles loads up to 1,800 watts, with cutoffs for overheating, overcurrent, and voltage problems. Its built-in LED can change color to reflect current energy use. It costs $19.99 in black or white.

If you know someone constantly struggling to make work from the road work, the Sennheiser MOMENTUM 5 Wireless headphones are an audio oasis they will appreciate for years to come. The hybrid noise cancellation, 8-band graphic EQ, Snapdragon Sound, and other personalization features cut the noise and sculpt the sound, perfect for open-office escapees and in-control commuters. And a long-haul battery life delivers up to 57 hours of runtime, so playlists won’t run out somewhere over the Atlantic. Plus, the battery is user-replaceable, reducing e-waste and extending ownership. This is the perfect gift for music-loving control freqs.

Sonos isn’t the only way to fill a house with speakers that talk to each other. Denon’s redesigned Home lineup runs on HEOS, which can link up to 64 speakers across a home, and the three sizes scale with the room. The $399 Home 200 plays stereo from three tweeters and a 4-inch woofer. The $599 Home 400 adds two upward-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos Music, and the $799 Home 600 packs eight drivers, including dual 6.5-inch woofers, each with its own amplifier. All three take Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB-C, and aux. The stone and charcoal finishes look more like something from a furniture store than an electronics aisle.

The Bose LifeStyle Ultra Home Theater Set is perfect for homes that struggle with the volume of content and components. From the soundbar to the wireless satellites and subwoofer, everything is compact and design-conscious, perfect for a minimalist who doesn’t want to sacrifice expression. Bose SpeechClarity uses AI enhancement to make dialogue more audible without having to ride the volume constantly. CustomTune calibrates immersion to the room’s actual acoustics. And when it’s not movie night, stream music via AirPlay 2/Google Cast, no app required. Add more speakers later for a multiroom setup, making this a great gift for someone who wants to scale up a whole-home setup without sacrificing space.

#4562. Tested: 2027 Audi Q9 Brings Big Space and Big Tech

The extra-large Q9 fills an obvious gap in Audi’s SUV lineup. Thankfully, it’s quite good to drive too.

The 2027 Audi Q9 probably should have gone on sale over a decade ago, but better late than never for the extra-long, three-row Audi SUV. Engineered and designed with space-craving Americans in mind, the Q9 clings to a sporty attitude all while nearly filling out the same footprint as a Chevrolet Tahoe. It’s a bit of a balancing act, but made a touch easier by launching with two different versions: Q9 and SQ9. You can read about the latter here, and while its V-8 is always going to be a temptation, the regular Q9 is all the three-row most buyers in this part of the market will need and more.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

The Q9 is no slouch in base form, which is only right considering the nearly-$90,000 starting price. There’s no pokey four-cylinder option; instead, it gets Audi’s potent 2.9-liter twin-turbo V-6 as the standard engine. This motor can be found all across the VW Group, but most notably in sportier offerings from Porsche and Audi. Here, it makes 429 hp and 442 lb-ft of torque. Audi channels this power through an eight-speed automatic transmission onward to all four wheels via the Quattro all-wheel-drive system. Audi claims a 0–60 time of only 4.9 seconds, and while that’s 1.1 seconds slower than the V-8-powered SQ9, any three-row SUV that gets to 60 in under five is worthy of celebrating.

Transmission: Eight-speed auto, all-wheel drive

Audis tend to have a universal sense of solidity from behind the wheel, and the Q9 adopts this familiar demeanor. It feels substantial on the road, in large part because it is. Even by the high standards of luxury three-rows, the Q9 has a commendable sense of isolation. Its multilink front and rear, paired with the standard air suspension and adaptive dampers, sop up poor pavement with the best of them, even riding on 22-inch wheels.

Despite not needing to be particularly agile, the Q9 was still ready to boogie when I flipped it into its Dynamic mode. Surprisingly, the Q9 and SQ9 share the same suspension, which results in the Q9 being nearly as fun to throw around as the SQ9. In one way, it’s actually better than its V-8-powered sibling: weight. The Q9 weighs a few hundred pounds less than the SQ9, and much of that difference is lifted off the front end. So on a twisty section of road, the Q9 responded with greater eagerness than I expected in something so large, and it definitely had a pointier front end than the SQ9.

That said, the regular Q9 also has a more laid-back tune to its Quattro system, one that isn’t as rear-biased as the SQ9’s. I had to be pushing hard to discern much of a difference on paved roads, though. Audi’s senior Quattro engineer, Dieter Weidemann, told me he actually prefers the base Q9’s Quattro system on low-grip surfaces. Something for potential buyers who regularly drive on snow to consider.

The V-6 itself is largely inoffensive outside of some input lag. It is quiet and got this beast up and moving with no wheezing or stress. Thank the peak torque hitting at a low 2000 rpm for that effortless acceleration sensation around town. Fuel economy isn’t out yet, and while it will surely be better than the thirsty SQ9, the V-6 is still going to drink premium fuel at copious rates.

Liking big screens is a prerequisite for loving the Q9’s interior. The monolithic structure that houses both the digital instrument cluster and infotainment system is the first thing you notice upon opening the door. It’s impressive from a size and screen quality perspective, but there’s a ton of wasted space with large areas of shiny black trim all around the displays.

Audi did well to resist an all-touch-control steering-wheel design, maintaining the all-important volume scroll wheel and buttons you can physically press to skip songs. The real tactile high point is the new turn signals that click with such authority and solidity thanks to their chunky design and easily learned action.

That turn signal is shared with other Audis, but high-class, flagship-esque moments can be found all throughout this interior. The Q9 is the first Audi to feature a new seat design that incorporates one of the most thorough massage functions in the game and 4D sound that lets you experience the music physically through speakers in the seats. Optional automatic doors (both front and rear) make opening and closing them a button-operated task, or you can nudge them to prompt the motors to activate. Considering the size and weight of the rear doors (that open a full 90 degrees), it’s a feature I suspect most owners will learn to like more over the course of ownership.

The second row can be made into a serious luxury abode by optioning the captain’s chairs instead of bench seating. These are powered bucket seats that hardly give up a lick of comfort compared to those in front, though I was disappointed to see they don’t feature the same massage/sound feature as the front buckets. When motored up and out of the way, they leave an adult human-size path into the third row, and there’s even room for that same adult to sit back there in relative comfort should you compromise the second-row legroom by a couple of inches. No, I wouldn’t choose a Q9 to haul six adults across the country, but it is well suited to shorter, fully-loaded drives. A four-zone climate-control system is standard, but there’s an available five-zone setup with an independently controlled zone for those in the wayback.

It’s this spacious third row and the cargo area behind it that finally bring Audi over the hump with its biggest SUV. The Q7 left space for kids, but no adult would ever want to spend time in the third row of that car. Now, you can get the Q9, fill it up with people, and still have a respectable amount of room behind that third row for necessary cargo. Just don’t expect Suburban levels of utility.

Audi isn’t aiming to be the sportiest in this segment, which is an honor that still belongs to the BMW X7. But the Q9 is coming to the fight with an armory of tech and good old-fashioned easy luxury. This is the type of car Audi should have built years ago. Better late than never.

But the cabin architecture struggles to scream flagship with a screen setup that’s verging on tacky, from the gauge cluster to the oddly integrated passenger screen. Odd packaging decisions like including two wireless phone chargers as opposed to storage areas seem like a miss for the American market. And this Q9 truly was designed and engineered for America, a fact Audi is happy to tout repeatedly.

The price is right where it needs to be compared to the BMW X7 and Mercedes-Benz GLS. There’s dynamic fun to be found should you want to find it, but the Q9 doesn’t compromise its ability to be a luxury family car for outright performance. That is surely the smart move here, and I suspect it’ll be the answer for far more folks than the compromised Q7.

The turn signals that project light onto the pavement to the left or right of the car at night are an awesome feature. With distracted driving an unfortunate reality, the better you’re able to get other people’s attention, the safer a lane change can be. Also it’s just flat-out cool that we’re able to project legible messages on the ground to communicate with other drivers on the road now.

#4561. Bigger, badder Section 179 tax deduction could POWER UP fleet electrification [update]

With national diesel prices inching towards $7/gallon and Tesla’s $290,000 Semi trucks finally making their way to paying customers, it’s worth revisiting how Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) helped beef up the Section 179 deduction, and look again at how it could help your fleet ditch diesel sooner rather than later.

At the core of this thinking is the fact that the IRS does not distinguish between fuel choices, so there’s no separate depreciation category for electric- vs. diesel-fueled commercial trucks. The relevant classifications, then, are the vehicle’s use and property classes, and under the IRS’ depreciation guidelines, tractor units designed for over-the-road use are classified as 3-year properties and fall under the 20-year recovery threshold for 100% bonus depreciation, Tesla’s electric Semi can benefit from 179 just like their diesel-powered competitors. But don’t get me wrong – this isn’t just great news for Tesla Semi buyers. Electric garbage trucks, electric vocational trucks, battery electric reefer trailers, and even some big electric forklifts can potentially benefit from the same accelerated depreciation rules, since the IRS lists these as, “specialized business vehicles,” with no distinction between electric, diesel, natural gas, hydrogen, magic pixie dust, anything else.

There’s been some additional movement on the tax front since our original article, too. Earlier this year, the IRS issued Notice 2026-11, providing additional guidance on the permanent restoration of 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025. That means that eligible businesses might be able to combine Section 179 expensing with bonus depreciation when ordering qualifying fleet equipment – and ordering is the key word. The IRS has specific rules for determining when equipment is considered acquired under a written, binding contract, and your tax professional and truck dealer can probably help you figure out a way to make those rules work in your favor.

You can check out the original article (with a few corrections sprinkled in to align with the latest guidance from Notice 2026-11 and Publication 946) below. Give it a read, read the disclaimer twice, then let us know what you think in the comments.

After the Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit (Section 45W) expired on September 30, the “experts” rushed out predictions of an EV sales slowdown in Q4. But, with over 6,800 pages in the Internal Revenue Code still in play, a turbocharged Section 179 tax deduction could still power a strong year for commercial EVs.

The One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025 gutted America’s energy independence goals and ensuring its auto industry would fall even further behind the Chinese in the EV race, but the loss of Section 45W wasn’t the only change written into the IRS’ rulebook. Section 179, an immediate expense reduction that business owners can take on depreciable equipment assets, has been made significantly more powerful for 2025.

The section 179 expense deduction is limited to such items as cars, office equipment, business machinery, and computers. This speedy deduction can provide substantial tax relief for business owners who are purchasing startup equipment.

The revised Section 179 tax credit (or, more accurately, expense reduction) allows for a 100% deduction for equipment purchases has doubled to $2.5 million, with a phase-out kicking in at $4 million of capital investments that drops to zero at $6.5 million. That can be applied to new and used vehicles, as well as charging infrastructure, battery energy storage systems, specialized tools, and more (as long as they’re new to you).

“But wait,” as they say. “There’s more!” A revised Section 168(k) also allows for bonus depreciation on eligible equipment and property, accelerating depreciation for a reduced tax burden.

Section 179 and bonus depreciation aren’t mutually exclusive, either, which means that businesses don’t have to exceed the Section 179 spending cap to be able to take advantage of both. A fleet operator can elect to expense a portion of a qualifying vehicle or equipment purchase under Section 179, then apply bonus depreciation to the remaining eligible basis.

With 100% bonus depreciation restored for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, that combination could allow businesses to deduct the entire qualifying business-use cost of an electric truck or other commercial equipment in the first year, subject to applicable eligibility requirements and limitations.

It’s a bit convoluted (what good tax code isn’t?), but these tax incentives are great for businesses looking to buy enough electric equipment assets to exceed the Section 179 spending limit – and, given the new Uber/Tesla semi truck purchase plan, the continued growth of the electric terminal tractor market, and the willingness of several utilities to incentivize both electric commercial vehicles and the deployment of smart EV charging infrastructure, that number may be bigger than you think.

Tax law is weird. Not only are there Federal tax laws and rules that need to be followed, but state and even local county and city rules, as well. As such, you want to make sure they don’t get you the way the got Capone.

Even worse, your favorite journalist (Hi!) is probably an idiot. Get a certified accountant and tax law expert to help walk you through the dirtier details of your specific scenario – but don’t let the complexity of human interaction slow you down, either. The really rich guys you know pay pennies on the tax dollar compared to you and me, because they’re not afraid to ask their accountants for help.

As a tax CPA, I cringe when I see "Sec 179" and the word "credit" put together. It is grossly inaccurate to say that Sec 179 is a tax credit.

Sec 179 and bonus depreciation are nothing new. OBBBA just raised the 179 maximum up, but the deductibility, specifically for heavy vehicles like semis, is unchanged.

The TL;DR version, though, is this: there’s still plenty of incentives out there for fleet operators looking to electrify their operations.

#4560. The grossest thing you touch every day, according to science

Published Nov 1, 2026 5:02 PM EST

It’s probably not something you want to think about, but what do you think is the dirtiest thing you touch every day? If you commute via subway, you might suspect a stairwell handle or train pole as the most likely culprit. If you go from your house to your car to an office, maybe it’s the elevator button or the key fob you have to dig out of your bag. All very good guesses–you might even be tempted to pull out your phone and look up the correct answer.

“It might surprise people, but the dirtiest thing they encounter every day is their own cellphone,” says Caitlin Mangan, a Lab Manager for Gillson Sciences. “People take them everywhere with them, including the bathroom. They are touched thousands of times a day, without people cleaning them or washing their hands in between tasks.”

The University of Michigan’s Institute for Healthcare Policy & Innovation puts it this way: Your cellphone is 10 times dirtier than a toilet seat. Yeah, that’s pretty gross.

The frequency of contact contributes to that grossness. The study shows that, on average, people check their phones 47 times a day. And like your clothing and shoes, you carry your beloved phone through various environments of differing cleanliness levels. In fact, that subway pole may actually be cleaner than your iPhone.

“It depends on how often the areas are cleaned,” says Mangan. “For example, an office building door handle typically has less people touching it day-to-day, but because of that it might not be cleaned as frequently and therefore has a high risk of having germs. Whereas a subway pole that is cleaned daily and properly sanitized will have less germs to transfer.”

Cellphones have been known to carry skin bacteria like Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, as well as fecal bacteria like E. coli and Enterococcus faecalis. These bacteria can cause skin infections, strep throat, or gastrointestinal illnesses producing nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. You can help yourself by avoiding using your phone in the restroom, not placing it down on surfaces where germs likely lurk, and when speaking into it, not letting it touch your cheek or mouth.

Of course, you should also clean your phone with paper towels, alcohol, and cotton swabs whenever possible and follow the number one rule of germ spread prevention: Wash your hands frequently and thoroughly.

#4559. Bald eagle mistaken for trashbag on the road to recovery

Published Nov 2, 2026 9:00 AM EST

A Pennsylvania resident recently arrived home to find what looked like an unassuming black trash bag in their yard. But the bag moved and lifted its head. Turns out, it was not a bag, but a bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus). And something was very wrong with her.

A state Game Warden brought the eagle to Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southern Pennsylvania to be checked out. The bird couldn’t stand and her legs were limp, which is a typical symptom of spinal trauma. Nonetheless, the team also tested the eagle for lead poisoning, and found that she indeed had lead in her system. Even though the eagle wasn’t showing signs of such poisoning, they weren’t surprised by these results.

In a 2022 study published in the journal Science, researchers investigated lead exposure in 1,210 bald and golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) in North America and found chronic lead poisoning in 46 to 47 percent of both eagles and acute lead poisoning in 27 to 33 percent of bald eagles. Lead exposure in eagles and other avian scavengers mostly occurs when they consume the remains of animals shot with lead ammunition and left behind by hunters.

“Lead poisoning is so common that even eagles brought in for other injuries are now routinely tested for it, and almost all show some level of lead in their system,” Tracie Young, Raven Ridge Wildlife Center director, tells Popular Science.

Even small quantities of lead can be extremely toxic. Lead poisoning can cause brain swelling, trouble breathing, weak muscles, dehydration, starvation, kidney and liver problems, or seizures, Young explains.

“Nerve damage can cause them to lose vision, coordination, and normal movement, so the bird may look ‘drunk’ or not be able to stand,” she continues. “When these eagles are starving, they lose their hunting skills and can’t catch food. As scavengers, they look for roadkill, but because they are uncoordinated, they often get hit by vehicles.”

It’s likely that this is what happened to the trash-bag-looking female eagle in Pennsylvania. At the wildlife center, she received chelation therapy for the lead poisoning. Chelation therapy involves the administration of administering specialized chemical agents that attach to the lead molecules in the bird’s blood and form a compound that is expelled, mostly via urine. The eagle also received physical therapy to regain strength in her legs and mitigate spinal pain and swelling.

Her rehabilitation process has been challenging, but not without its rewards. She is currently able to stand and lives in an outdoor area with an open space where she can continue her rehabilitation process. The eagle is a good candidate for release, but Young says she will require weeks of flight training.

“We urge all hunters and anglers to make a crucial choice: opt for lead-free ammunition and lead-free fishing gear,” the wildlife center wrote in a Facebook post. “This single decision at checkout can significantly improve the lives of countless eagles and other wildlife suffering from lead poisoning.”

#4558. Peterbilt makes it easier than ever for government fleets to go electric

Legendary truck brand Peterbilt is lowering procurement barriers for state and municipal fleets looking to electrify their assets by adding its growing lineup of medium- and heavy-duty battery electric trucks to its cooperative purchasing Agreement with Sourcewell.

The expanded purchasing contract, extended through July 2028, provides Sourcewell’s more than 50,000 member organizations access to competitively solicited contracts with pre-negotiated pricing and terms across the Peterbilt brand’s full lineup of Class 5-8 commercial trucks. That contract allows eligible agencies to streamline procurement by sourcing Peterbilt’s on-highway, vocational and medium-duty BEVs through Sourcewell’s pre-negotiated agreement, potentially eliminating the need to go through a long, agonizing bidding process of their own.

“Our long-standing relationship with Sourcewell reflects Peterbilt’s commitment to delivering solutions tailored to the unique needs of public fleets,” explains Erik Johnson, assistant general manager of sales and marketing at Peterbilt. “By adding our electric vehicles to the contract and eliminating lengthy bidding processes, we’re helping organizations maximize uptime and invest their resources where it matters most, keeping their communities running.”

I hear some of you asking, “Why is this important, and what exactly is Sourcewell?” And you’re very smart to ask.

See, when your state or local government decides it needs a new truck, it can’t just call up someone’s cousin and cut an inflated check backed by your tax dollars (regardless of what you saw on Fox News). Instead, public agencies generally have to follow competitive purchasing rules that are designed to ensure fairness, transparency, and responsible use of taxpayer money. That can mean writing and publishing a request for proposals (RFP), publicly soliciting bids, evaluating competing offers, and even allowing public comments that can all-too easily devolve into 17 hours of Pawnee-level discourse among stakeholders (real and imagined) about the relative merits of competing proposals.

Sourcewell is a government agency that basically does all that ahead of time, publishing RFPs, soliciting ,and evaluating bids against established criteria, then awarding contracts through a transparent, auditable process that makes competitively negotiated pricing available to more than 50,000 government, education and nonprofit organizations across the US and Canada.

In practice, that means your local government fleets can leverage Sourcewell to quickly adapt to pressing needs in a way that doesn’t bypass the bidding process (which would be illegal), but which effectively says, “we trust Sourcewell’s process.”

You can check out the full text of Sourcewell’s contract with Peterbilt, below, then let us know what you think of Pete’s efforts to electrify your local government fleet in the comments.

#4557. Estaban Ocon Removed from Mexico City Grand Prix; Ryō Hirakawa Set for F1 Debut with Haas

Estaban Ocon, already out with Haas at the end of the year, was pulled out of the Grand Prix weekend with no further statement from Haas.

The TGR Haas F1 Team shared on social media early Sunday morning that Esteban Ocon would be replaced by Ryō Hirakawa for the remainder of the weekend.

Hirakawa already drove in Free Practice 1 ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix in a 10-rookie-stacked field, finishing 15th-fastest overall and fifth-fastest among the rookies.

This will be Hirakawa’s F1 debut, a week before he battles with his Toyota Gazoo Racing teammates for the 2026 driver title in the World Endurance Challenge. Hirakawa is a two-time 24 Hours of Le Mans winner and has served as Haas’ reserve driver since 2025.

Hirakawa becomes the oldest driver to start their first F1 race since Andre Lotterer in the 2014 Belgian Grand Prix, who was filling in for Hirakawa’s now WEC Toyota teammate Kamui Kobayashi.

Hirakawa was one of the names reportedly shortlisted for Ocon’s seat in 2027 before it ultimately went to Rafael Câmara.

This weekend, the F1 paddock has already seen two drivers sidelined with illness, with Kimi Antonelli stepping away from a championship being allowed out of media availability with a viral bug, followed by hometown hero Sergio Perez having to sit out Friday.

But Haas has not released whether Ocon’s absence is for a similar reason and says that ‘no further statements will be made at this time.’

The decision could be the end of Ocon’s time at Haas, and with WEC Monza and F1 Brazil next weekend, Hirakawa will have a scheduling conflict if he’s chosen to complete the year in the Haas seat. Hirakawa is on the No. 8 TR010 driver lineup that currently leads the WEC championship over the NO. 7 sister car.

#4555. Clerical Error Means Herta is Still One Point Shy of Super License Following Mexico FP1

One extra step is added to Colton Herta’s journey to F1, following a miscalculation of superlicense points stemming from an IndyCar.com clerical error.

Colton Herta participated in back-to-back Grand Prix Free Practice 1 sessions in Austin and Mexico City, hoping to secure the final superlicense points to potentially move into Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac in 2027.

Cadillac has only confirmed Sergio Perez’s contract extension, as a driver change seems imminent for Bottas ride.

The problem is that, at the start of Herta’s 2026 F2 campaign, the FIA noted he had 35 points toward his license from his last three years of IndyCar competition; at some point, this number was upped to 36 when he truly had 35. A misprint on the IndyCar website had Herta finishing sixth in the championship instead of seventh in 2025. Herta was projected to finish sixth last year, but Felix Rosenqvist's late-season push brought him to sixth in the points instead.

“There was an anomaly in the website database display, which was caught this week and now reflects the official standings as they were published Aug. 31, 2025,” IndyCar said in a statement.

The championship finishes were shown in error at some point over the spring when the FIA did it’s fact-checking and did not look into it again until this weekend, with the 40-point goal in sight.

The FIA used ‘The Way Back Machine’, an online resource to help figure out how they got the math wrong. It showed that the championship standings were changed incorrectly at one point during the summer, but they were correct at the start of the year.

“Obviously, we were still doing our meetings and whatnot, so I haven't talked to anybody about it,” Herta told media in Mexico City. “As far as I was concerned, going into the weekend, if I did 100km here, I would have 40.”

Herta has struggled in F2, so his only points this year have come from practice sessions. All F1 teams must put rookies in at least four practice sessions over the course of the season. Cadillac has already used one extra session to help Herta reach the superlicence goal, and his Monza run this September wasn't long enough to count for a point. Cadillac must run Herta in one more free practice before the year’s end. Next weekend in Brazil is an easy option, with a lack of support races.

#4554. Yes, electric motorcycles will replace gasoline motorcycles, but not the way you think

For years, the conventional wisdom surrounding electric motorcycles has been fairly straightforward: Build an electric motorcycle that’s just as good as a gasoline-powered motorcycle, make it affordable enough, and eventually riders will switch.

It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed. Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.

But I think we’ve been looking at electric motorcycles all wrong. Because the future of electric motorcycles isn’t necessarily about convincing today’s gasoline motorcycle riders to switch. It’s about the next generation of riders who won’t have any reason to start with gasoline in the first place.

And that’s a much bigger deal than it might sound. In fact, it’s the entire key to the puzzle. Because make no mistake, the future of motorcycling is electric. It just won’t happen the way most people think.

The problem with applying the electric car playbook to motorcycles is that motorcycles aren’t cars.

For most people, a car is a tool. It’s transportation. Sure, some drivers are deeply passionate about their cars, but they are a minority. The vast majority simply want something comfortable, reliable, affordable, and convenient to get them from point A to point B.

Motorcycles, especially in markets like the US and Europe, are different. In fact, it’s the complete opposite of the car situation. For a minority of Western riders, and especially American riders, a motorcycle is a tool. For the vast majority, it’s a passion. People generally buy motorcycles because they love motorcycles. And for many riders, that love is deeply intertwined with the gasoline engine itself.

The sound, the vibration, the shifting, the mechanical character. These aren’t necessarily flaws to be engineered away. They’re part of the experience for traditional riders.

You can show someone like that an electric motorcycle with better acceleration, lower maintenance costs, cheaper operating expenses, and the convenience of charging at home, and they still won’t want it.

Not because the electric motorcycle isn’t good enough, but because it isn’t what they love.

And that’s fine. There’s nothing wrong with loving gasoline motorcycles if that’s your thing. But it means that trying to convert those riders may be a losing battle, at least on any meaningful timeline.

Unfortunately though, it seems many years were wasted on that approach. Take Harley-Davidson, for example.

The brand started building its first electric motorcycle over a decade ago – commendable among all the other legacy motorcycle manufacturers that turned their noses up at the thought of going electric. When it was released in 2018, the Harley-Davidson LiveWire received rave reviews, but it just didn’t sell well. For one, it was insanely expensive at $30,000. But the other major reason was that no matter how amazing it was, it wasn’t going to scratch that gasoline itch that most riders still had.

That motorcycle still exists in small-scale production as the LiveWire One through H-D’s electric spinoff, but now LiveWire has wisened up to the real pathway to moving higher numbers of electric motorcycles with its S4 Honcho line. And this brings us to how electric motorcycles will really replace their gasoline counterparts.

Now consider what’s happening with younger riders today.

Millions of people are growing up riding electric bicycles, electric scooters, and increasingly powerful e-motos. For them, electric two-wheelers aren’t some strange new alternative to the real thing. They are the real thing.

They’ve grown accustomed to instant torque, quiet operation, and the simplicity of twisting a throttle and going. To these riders, a gasoline-powered motorcycle is laughably primitive. It’d be like me handing you a gasoline-powered drill or blender. Yeah, exactly. Now look who’s suddenly on team battery, eh?

So now we have a whole new generation of riders getting ready to come of age. And eventually, many of those riders are going to want something more.

Maybe they’ve spent years riding a 28 mph electric bike, or a 40 mph electric moto. Now they’re young adults, they want to ride on faster roads, and they want something capable of 70 or 80 mph that’s actually street legal. They’ve gone from a sixteen-year-old in a hoodie to a twenty-six-year-old in a collared shirt. Instead of getting to high school, now they’re getting to work. But they haven’t lost that desire to ride.

It’s not because they’ve carefully compared electric and gasoline motorcycles and decided that electric is superior. It’s not because they’re trying to save the planet or reduce their maintenance costs. It’s simply because they grew up with electric two-wheelers as the norm.

It’s simply the next logical step in the type of riding they’ve already been doing for years.

Will a few of them transition over to gasoline-powered motorcycles? Sure. But for most, gasoline motorcycles will never even enter the equation.

Don’t get me wrong, we haven’t seen the last of gasoline motorcycles.

And I don’t even think electric motorcycles are going to suddenly outsell gasoline motorcycles because they become objectively better machines. At least not in the traditional recreational motorcycle markets we’re talking about here.

Instead, I think we’re going to see a somewhat more gradual generational transition.

Today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts will largely keep riding gasoline motorcycles. They’ll keep buying them, maintaining them, and enjoying them for as long as they can.

But as those riders age out of motorcycling, the next generation won’t replace them with another generation of gasoline motorcycle buyers. In other words, gasoline motorcycles will die out with their riders.

Increasingly, those younger riders will have already entered the world of powered two-wheelers through electric bikes and e-motos. When they’re ready to move up, electric motorcycles will be waiting for them.

And over those next few years, the technology will only become better. The only remaining Achilles’ heel of electric motorcycles – their run time – will get better and better as battery technology improves and we move towards solid-state batteries.

Suddenly they’ll be on par with gasoline motorcycles for range and ‘fueling’ time, yet will beat those combustion bikes elsewhere. But at that point, “better” won’t even matter anymore as electrics will be the only comfortable option for the vast majority of new riders. Again, you wouldn’t buy a power drill that runs on a gasoline engine when you’ve seen how convenient and effective a lithium-ion power drill has been your whole life.

Over time, the traditional gasoline motorcycle market will simply shrink as its existing customer base gets older, while electric motorcycles build an entirely new customer base alongside it.

And again, there will be exceptions in both directions. Some lifelong gasoline riders will enthusiastically embrace electric motorcycles, and some younger riders will still discover the appeal of combustion engines and running through the gears.

Living in SE Asia this all sounds very strange. The vast majority of the worlds bikes are not owned as toys, they are the main form of transport for the family. I agree with a lot of the article but Asia is already years ahead. The fuel shortages and sky high prices are pushing people electric far faster than riders are "aging out"

But the broader trend will be driven less by conversion and more by generational replacement.

That’s why electric motorcycles will eventually become the standard, even if they never manage to convince most of today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts to switch.

Gasoline motorcycles won’t necessarily disappear because electric motorcycles finally beat them at their own game. They’ll fade because the next generation of riders will be playing a different game entirely.

In other words, and to paraphrase T. S. Eliot, gasoline motorcycles won’t go out with a bang, but with a whimper.

#4553. A bull and a male donkey’s sexual relationship turns heads

Published Nov 2, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Sex between two animals of the same sex is widespread. Over 1,000 animal species from nematode worms to penguins to cattle all dabble in same-sex interactions. But a relationship between a bull named Achille and a male donkey named Patrocolo is raising eyebrows. The pair lives on a plateau in Ethiopia, and both could have chosen partners of the opposite sex and same species on numerous occasions. However, they continued to choose each other, despite belonging to different owners and only seeing one another when spending time in a pasture. A study published today in the journal Current Biology chronicles this surprising union.

“The sexual interactions between Achille, the bull, and Patroclo, the male donkey, were not isolated events,” Elisabetta Palagi, a study co-author and evolutionary biologist at the Università di Pisa (UNIPI) in Italy, said in a statement. “What really caught our attention was that these interactions were embedded in a very selective and consistent social relationship between the two individuals.”

The team first spotted these interactions while conducting another study earlier this year. They saw Achille mounting Patroclo, and were surprised to see that Patroclo did not try to avoid the bull, kick him, or show any defensive reactions.

“They repeatedly chose to stay close to each other and engaged in many different affiliative behaviors, such as licking, rubbing, and nuzzling, alongside the repeated mounting behavior,” added co-author André da Cruz, a PhD student at UNIPI. “Importantly, this was happening in a social environment where both animals had access to other potential partners, including individuals of both sexes and of their own species.”

The team recorded all of the interactions they witnessed involving either Achille or Patroclo. In total, the observed 51 mountings between the male bull and donkey from March 6 to March 19. In these interactions, Patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and then nipped at the bull. They repeatedly directed most of their sexual and social interactions toward each other, and the team reported no indication from the bull or donkey that either wished to discourage those advances. Achille mounted another male donkey only twice, and that other male showed avoidance behaviors and threatening expressions, like flattened ears.

“We believe the key finding is not simply that a bull mounted a male donkey,” said study co-author Martina Francesconi, also a PhD student at UNIPI. “It is that this unusual sexual behavior was part of a broader, selective social relationship. Our observations suggest that it cannot be easily explained simply by a lack of alternative mating opportunities, although we cannot say from this study exactly what function these sexual interactions may have had.”

According to the team, these observations have wider implications for our understanding of how sexual behavior is a complex social trait that goes beyond its role in reproduction. It also raises important questions for future studies, including if these interactions are primarily related to social bonding, what the benefits are, and if they play a role in reducing tension or maintaining relationships. In previous studies, same-sex mounting in nonhuman primates appears to be a form of conflict resolution and way to strengthen bonds, and may help male macaques reproduce more successfully.

“More broadly, we would like to better understand how social relationships shape sexual behavior and how behavioral flexibility allows animals to navigate complex social environments,” said Palagi. “We see this study as a starting point for asking these broader questions.”

#4552. Aloe found in ancient Egyptian mummy skull

Published Nov 2, 2026 12:58 PM EST

Archaeologists have identified a previously undocumented ingredient used in ancient Egyptian mummifications—and a famous medieval medicine concocted from the mummies themselves. At Germany’s Marburg University, researchers pinpointed traces of aloe-associated plant material in a 2,700-year-old mummy skull, and a popular centuries’ old apothecary cure-all known as Mumia vera aegyptiaca.

There is no one way to make a mummy. Mummification methods have varied across the world for thousands of years, even within a single culture. Ancient Egyptians honed their own processes over generations, and archaeologists are still sifting through millennia’s worth of artifacts and texts to better understand the iconic postmortem procedures.

Egyptology first truly took off in Europe during the late 18th century, but people’s fascination with mummies goes much further back in time. However, the long and complex medicinal history of mummy-derived treatments collectively called Mumia likely began as a 12th century mistranslation. Persian pharmacists often used a black pitch called mumiya in wound care, which medieval translators of Latin later mistook for similarly dark materials used in Egyptian mummification. This eventually led to an entire trade network centered on the import of powdered mummy remains sold by apothecaries as a Mumia cure-all—and sometimes even an aphrodisiac—for centuries.

Archaeologists have already documented many mummification ingredients derived from various minerals, animals, and plants. These span a range of coniferous tars and reins, oils, fats, beeswax, and bitumen, as well as rarer regional plant distillations like dammar and elemi. Knowing there is still much more to learn, the team at Marburg University recently analyzed 24 historically related objects stored at various institutions. These included an Egyptian mummified skull dated to the 8th century BCE, as well as an 18th century historical preparation of Mumia housed at Heidelberg Pharmacy Museum.

Their findings were recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and offer the first molecular evidence of mummy-related materials directly derived from aloe. This is particularly important, since “aloe” often historically referred to a variety of plants like agarwood outside the Aloe genus. According to Tanja Pommerening, a study co-author and director of Marburg University’s Institute for the History of Pharmacy and Medicine, the detection of aloe in Mumia is also particularly significant. Prior to this study, many researchers assumed medieval authors drew their Mumia recipes from biblical passages. These include John 19:39, which references a “mixture of myrrh and aloes.”

“The new findings suggest that this association may have deeper historical roots,” explained Pommerening.

However, since only two of the 24 artifacts in the study yielded traces of aloe, the frequency of the plant’s use in mummification and Mumia remains unclear. It’s possible that preparers may have only incorporated the material during certain historical periods, or depending on its availability. Still, Pommerening and her colleagues plan to continue similar examinations of other historical objects.

“Our goal is not only to analyze the chemical composition of ancient medicines and embalming materials, but also to gain a deeper understanding of their production, use, historical transmission, and cultural context,” added study co-author and Marburg University biologist Raphael Reher.

#4551. Isack Hadjar Warned Following Incident with Fan in Mexico City Paddock

The Red Bull driver received a formal warning after pushing away a fan who approached him in an “aggressive manner”.

Isack Hadjar was issued a formal warning from the Stewards following a fan interaction as he was heading to FP1 on Friday of the Mexico City Grand Prix Weekend.

Hadjar was running late for FP1 after stopping to take a photo with a young fan when an adult fan tried to grab him to take a selfie too. Hadjar pushed the fan away and kept moving forward.

The incident was caught on tape and reported to the FIA, and Hadjar was called to the Stewards.

In the meeting, Hadjar explained the situation, saying the guest approached him aggressively, and he responded by “placing his hand on the waist of the guest and holding him at bay, then [he] pushed him aside with his open right hand.”

The FIA says the second part of this move breached regulations, but it reduced the penalty to a formal warning based on five mitigating factors.

The Stewards reported that the factors were as follows:

a) The driver was reacting to an uninvited and rather aggressive action by another person.

b) The driver was [endeavoring] to make his way to the start of FP1 through a congested area.

c) The driver did not have sufficient security present.

d) The guest was invading his personal space without his consent.

e) The general issue drivers have experienced moving through the Paddock.

No fine or penalty points were levied against Hadjar for these reasons.

#4550. Dinosaur blood found in fossils for the first time

Published Nov 2, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Paleontologists regularly discover fossilized dinosaur bones, but they sometimes locate footprints and prehistoric shells. On rare occasions, researchers have even identified the ancient indentations of a dinosaur’s skin or feathers. But fossilized cells? Researchers have long assumed such microscopic levels of preservation were impossible. But, once again, nature has proven otherwise.

In a study published today in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), an international team of paleontologists confirmed the presence of intact biomolecules and mineralized red blood cells inside fossils of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur. Although previous work has suggested similar possibilities, the team’s research is the first to chemically identify oxygen-carrying blood compounds known as heme.

“This really is a landmark discovery,” Kliti Grice, a study co-author and chemist at Curtin University in Australia, said in a statement. “These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time.”

The evidence exists inside the fossilized limb bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali. Discovered in 2008, A. museunacionali was an Early Cretaceous theropod that lived in present-day northeastern Brazil. The fossils suggest a dinosaur measuring over 10 feet long and weighing about 75 pounds, but given its young age, A. museunacionali likely grew even larger.

After carefully examining thin slices of the fossils, paleontologists located the mineralized red blood cell molecular components, along with a complex manganese oxide called hausmannite. This material helped maintain the cellular structures of heme, a ring-shaped molecule that contains iron and binds many proteins, especially hemoglobin. The hausmannite also helped preserve additional biomolecules found in the blood, such as the amino acids in collagen. The study’s authors theorize this level of preservation could only occur following a rapid burial in an environment that was rich in microbes, but low in oxygen at the same time.

Grice and her collaborators said that their discovery has wider implications for molecular-level paleontology. Further study could help advance our understanding of blood’s evolution, dinosaur metabolism, and ancient animals’ activity levels. The knowledge that this type of preservation is possible at all could even extend far beyond Earth. If such delicate biomolecules fossilize over millions of years in harsh environments, then it’s possible similar traces of life may linger elsewhere in the universe.

#4549. Lewis Hamilton’s Secures First Ferrari Grand Prix Pole in CDMX

A three-year drought ends as Lewis Hamilton takes pole position for the Mexico City Grand Prix.

For the first time since Budapest in 2023, Lewis Hamilton is on pole for an F1 Grand Prix, taking pole for the Mexico City Grand Prix by 0.009 seconds over Mercedes’s George Russell.

This is Hamilton’s 105th GP pole and his first with Ferrari. Lewis Hamilton started on pole for a sprint earlier this year at Silverstone but was still awaiting the elusive GP pole. Hamilton won his first Grand Prix with Ferrari at the Catalunya-Barcelona Grand Prix in June.

Ferrari is the third team that Hamilton has won pole for, with his first 26 poles coming with McLaren, then 78 with Mercedes, and now one with Ferrari.

Hamilton looked set to place only one lap in Q3, going out with more than 10 minutes remaining. Instead, he came back out for a second run to advance from fourth, 0.422 seconds down from his teammate Charles Leclerc on Provisional pole, to take the top spot. Leclerc will start third behind Russell.

This is Hamilton’s second pole in Mexico City, with the first coming in 2016.

“Oh man, I'm lost for words,” Hamilton said post-quali. “It's been a really, really tough, challenging weekend. Obviously, P1, we had a rake running, and we obviously then had the engine issue we had yesterday, which meant that we were just on the back foot. I didn't get to do a long run, but we've really done a really good job with the setup over the weekend. We've already worked. We learned a lot from the last race, but it's so close between us all. And for example, Q2, I didn't get my lap at the beginning.

Ferrari did run through five sets of soft tires to get to Hamilton’s maiden pole, meaning that the competitors around him and Leclerc will have an advantage at the start of Sunday’s Grand Prix.

“I think the others have a new tire for the start, but wow, to have pole here, I mean, I don't even know if I've had a pole here before,” Hamilton said. “So it feels special to be in Mexico and get that. I think that's my first pole with Ferrari and 105. I like that number.”

Max Verstappen was the fourth-fastest but will start fifth after a one-place grid penalty handed to him and Liam Lawson for their avoidable crash in the stadium section during FP2 on Friday. Verstappen had the chance at a front-row qualifying spot but locked up in turn 13 on his final lap.

Kimi Antonelli qualified fifth and will start fourth. The young Italian driver needs only a ninth-place finish to claim the 2026 World Drivers' Championship. Reigning WDC champion, at least for one more day, Lando Norris bailed on his second lap in Q3 after a strong opening sector and will start sixth.

Red Bulls’ Isack Hadjar will start seventh, qualifying one spot ahead of the two Racing Bulls drivers. Lawson drops from eighth to ninth with his grid penalty, and his teammate Arvid Lindblad reaps the benefit. Pierre Gasly will start in tenth as the last driver to make it into Q3.

#4548. Watchful mama bear Gemini wins 2026 Helicopter Mom Award

Published Nov 2, 2026 4:07 PM EST

Even bears can be helicopter parents. The term coined in the 1990s by child development researchers Foster Cline and Jim Fay describes overly cautious parents who constantly monitor, control, and hover over (like a helicopter) their children’s activities out of fear.

For these watchful tendencies, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska has awarded a brown bear (Ursus arctos) named Gemini with the 2026 Helicopter Mom Award.

“We understand her choice, weighing the dangers of being around other bears at a prime fishing location,” the rangers write. “Still, we hope we see a lot more of them next year.”

The numbers also back up Gemini and other mother bears’ watchfulness. Brown bear cubs in Alaska have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent depending on the location. Gemini has also had cubs in 2023 and 2024.

The Rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The vast area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their beefy counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here exhibits their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4547. Leclerc Given FIA Minimum Penalty for Leaving the Track and Taking the Lead at the Mexico City GP

Neither his teammate nor Max Verstappen is happy that the FIA chose not to give Charles Leclerc a 10-second penalty for his opening-lap move.

At the start of the Mexico City Grand Prix, Charles Leclerc moved up from third to challenge his teammate Lewis Hamilton for the lead. And as has often been the case between the two Ferrari drivers this year, the battle could’ve gone cleaner.

Charles Leclerc took the lead by leaving the track in turn four, pushing Hamilton off his line and sending the pole-sitter tumbling back to third, with Max Verstappen taking advantage.

Quickly, Leclerc pulled out to a one-second lead over Verstappen. Leclerc had until turn 12 to give back the position, but with Verstappen down, he would drop from the lead to third.

Leclerc stayed in the lead, and the Stewards investigated his pass; recently, the FIA has had a stern talk with drivers and said that nearly every advantage gained by leaving the track that the driver did not reverse in time would result in a ten-second penalty.

Leclerc received a 5-second penalty, which was relayed over the radio to the drivers once he was 3.6 seconds clear of Verstappen and 5.1 seconds clear of his teammate Hamilton.

The mitigating circumstances for the league minimum of 5 seconds seem to be the nature of the opening turns at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

“Ha, I thought all the new penalties were a ten?” Verstappen replied over the radio to the news.

Neither Hamilton nor Leclerc ended up winning the race, with Hamilton finishing second and Leclerc fourth.

With his podium finish, Hamilton was asked about missing out on the win because of his teammate’s move and unwillingness to give back the position which ultimately led to a Ferrari loss.

“I mean, in the drivers' briefing we discussed that as soon as you go off in turn one, you have to give the position back, but obviously.” Hamilton referred to Leclerc’s 5-second penalty, “Last year I got a 10-second penalty for that same move that he did. But ultimately, it was that that cost us the win today. And I think we have to have some serious talks behind the scenes for sure.”

Post-race in the press conference, Hamilton expanded on his issue with Leclerc’s first-lap move and his subsequent move on the red-flag restart, saying that it has more to do with mentality than age.

“The guy’s 28 years old, so I don’t think it’s an age thing. I think it’s a mentality thing. It’s like do-or-die: either I win, or none of us do, and it shouldn’t be that. It should be us getting that one-two.”

With Hamilton in second place in the WDC challenge ahead of a Mercedes, his bitterness towards teamwork has grown over the season.
